c-census-gb-1801.text: Britain's Census Act was made law by royal assent on 31 December 1800, and the first census, in 1801, found the population of England and Wales to be 8.9 million, not counting those at sea, in the military, or prisoners.
c-census-gb-1801.label: approx
c-census-gb-1801.note: The count left out sailors, soldiers and prisoners, so the true population was somewhat higher.

c-census-us-1790.text: The United States census began in 1790 as a simple headcount, used to set the number of seats each state was to have in the House of Representatives.
c-census-us-1790.label: consensus

c-mpd-2023-coverage.text: The Maddison Project Database 2023, compiled by Jutta Bolt and Jan Luiten van Zanden, covers 169 countries and the period up to 2022.
c-mpd-2023-coverage.label: consensus

c-mpd-1820-acceleration.text: The 2023 Maddison update finds that 'pockets of economic growth existed before 1820', but that 'the world economy only started to accelerate after that year'.
c-mpd-1820-acceleration.label: approx
c-mpd-1820-acceleration.note: New (2024). The finding rests on reconstructed figures (see the method claims on this page).

c-mpd-indirect-method.text: For earlier periods there are no official statistics that fully cover the components of GDP, so economic historians reconstruct it, often by an indirect method that links real wages and levels of urbanization.
c-mpd-indirect-method.label: consensus

c-mpd-benchmark-2025.text: Long-run comparisons depend on the benchmark year used to compare prices; Bolt and van Zanden (2025) conclude that 'the best way forward for the Maddison Project is to stick to the original 1990 benchmark', 'yet with two important changes': the 2011 benchmark for the period after 1990, and a new historical benchmark for the US/UK comparison in 1909.
c-mpd-benchmark-2025.label: debated
c-mpd-benchmark-2025.note: Different benchmarks give different relative incomes; Bolt and van Zanden defend the 1990 benchmark, while critics such as Rafael Guthmann question how the series is built.

c-mpd-guthmann-2025.text: Rafael Guthmann (2025) argues that the Maddison Project's methods 'often differ over time and between countries', and that its data sets 'overestimate economic growth after 1950'.
c-mpd-guthmann-2025.label: debated
c-mpd-guthmann-2025.note: Guthmann's critique; Bolt and van Zanden defend a series anchored on a common benchmark.

c-mpd-gdppc-1750-1913.text: In the Maddison Project Database 2023, GDP per person in international dollars at 2011 prices was: United Kingdom 2,702 (1750), 3,306 (1820), 8,212 (1913); United States 2,674 (1820), 10,108 (1913); France 1,743, 1,809 and 5,555; China 1,061, 882 and 985; India 1,068, 937 and 1,073. In 1800 the Netherlands, at 4,184, stood above the United Kingdom, at 3,343.
c-mpd-gdppc-1750-1913.label: approx
c-mpd-gdppc-1750-1913.note: Reconstructed estimates, not measurements; they depend on the methods and the benchmark year discussed on this page. Figures downloaded from Our World in Data.

c-kant-enlightenment-1784.text: In his essay of 1784 Kant wrote that 'Enlightenment is man's emergence from his self-imposed nonage', and gave it the motto Sapere aude, dare to know. Kant had taught at the Albertina, the university of Königsberg, since 1755.
c-kant-enlightenment-1784.label: consensus

c-locke-liberal-source.text: Locke's Second Treatise of Government is 'the classical source of modern liberal political theory'.
c-locke-liberal-source.label: consensus

c-montesquieu-spirit-1748.text: Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws, first published in 1748, argued, in Britannica's words, that the three powers of government 'must be confided to different individuals or bodies, acting independently'; the Stanford Encyclopedia credits him with 'the basic structure and justification for the balance of political powers' that shaped James Madison.
c-montesquieu-spirit-1748.label: consensus

c-rousseau-direct-democracy.text: In William Bristow's summary, Rousseau argues that 'direct (pure) democracy is the only form of government in which human freedom can be realized'.
c-rousseau-direct-democracy.label: consensus

c-scottish-enlightenment.text: The Scottish Enlightenment included Hutcheson, Adam Smith, Hume and Reid.
c-scottish-enlightenment.label: consensus

c-smith-wealth-1776.text: Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations (1776) describes a pin factory in which 10 persons, by specializing, turn out 48,000 pins a day, and is a polemic against the restrictive measures of the 'mercantile system'.
c-smith-wealth-1776.label: consensus

c-mendelssohn-jerusalem-1783.text: Moses Mendelssohn (1729-1786) translated the Pentateuch and the Psalms into German; in Jerusalem (Berlin, 1783), in Dahlstrom's summary, he argued that 'neither the state nor religion can legitimately coerce human conscience', and in 1784 he wrote his own essay on what it means to enlighten.
c-mendelssohn-jerusalem-1783.label: consensus

c-israel-radical-moderate.text: Jonathan Israel divides the Enlightenment into a 'radical' camp and a 'moderate' one; the publisher's description of his Radical Enlightenment places stress on 'the pivotal role of Spinoza'. Anthony La Vopa (2009) calls the division an 'oversimplified classification' of thinkers and Israel's method 'fundamentally unhistorical'.
c-israel-radical-moderate.label: debated
c-israel-radical-moderate.note: Israel says his work has 'historicized our understanding' of the Enlightenment; La Vopa disagrees.

c-enlightenment-eurocentrism.text: In William Bristow's words, 'Enlightenment writings are rife with rank ethno- and Eurocentrism, often explicit.'
c-enlightenment-eurocentrism.label: debated
c-enlightenment-eurocentrism.note: How far this defines the Enlightenment is disputed; Sankar Muthu stresses thinkers who opposed empire.

c-muthu-against-empire.text: Sankar Muthu (2003) argues that Diderot, Kant and Herder argued against empire; the publisher's description says they defended 'the freedom of non-European peoples to order their own societies'.
c-muthu-against-empire.label: debated
c-muthu-against-empire.note: Muthu's reading of a minority strand; it does not deny the Eurocentrism of many other Enlightenment writings.

c-kleingeld-kant-race.text: Pauline Kleingeld (2007) argues that in the 1790s 'Kant radically changed his mind' and dropped his racial hierarchy.
c-kleingeld-kant-race.label: debated
c-kleingeld-kant-race.note: Kleingeld says her account departs from the standard view that Kant's position on race did not change.

c-amrev-proclamation-1763.text: The royal Proclamation of 7 October 1763 ordered the colonies to 'cease granting lands west of the peaks of the Appalachian Mountains'; Max Edelson writes that it 'marked the beginning of a process of escalating colonial dissent'.
c-amrev-proclamation-1763.label: consensus

c-amrev-declaration-1776.text: The Declaration of Independence, dated 4 July 1776, holds 'that all men are created equal' and accuses the King of inciting 'the merciless Indian Savages'. It and the Constitution of 1787 were both signed in Independence Hall in Philadelphia.
c-amrev-declaration-1776.label: consensus

c-amrev-constitution-slavery-1787.text: The Constitution, signed on 17 September 1787, apportioned representatives and direct taxes by counting free persons, 'excluding Indians not taxed, three fifths of all other Persons'; it barred Congress from prohibiting the slave trade 'prior to the Year one thousand eight hundred and eight'; and it required that any 'Person held to Service or Labour in one State' who escaped to another be delivered up.
c-amrev-constitution-slavery-1787.label: consensus

c-amrev-constitution-slavery-debate.text: Historians disagree about how far the Constitution protected slavery. In the publisher's description of his book, Sean Wilentz shows the framers choosing to 'abide slavery without legitimizing it'; the description of David Waldstreicher's book says that 'Slavery was as important to the making of the Constitution as the Constitution was to the survival of slavery.'
c-amrev-constitution-slavery-debate.label: debated
c-amrev-constitution-slavery-debate.note: Wilentz (2019) stresses that the framers refused to recognise 'property in man' in the text; Waldstreicher (2010) stresses the clauses that protected slaveholders.

c-amrev-bill-of-rights-1791.text: The Bill of Rights was ratified on 15 December 1791; its First Amendment begins 'Congress shall make no law respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof'.
c-amrev-bill-of-rights-1791.label: consensus

c-amrev-loyalist-exodus.text: According to Maya Jasanoff, some 60,000 American loyalists fled after the war, taking with them 15,000 slaves.
c-amrev-loyalist-exodus.label: approx
c-amrev-loyalist-exodus.note: Jasanoff's estimates; the numbers are rounded.

c-amrev-bailyn-1967.text: Bernard Bailyn (1967), reading the pamphlets of the period, argued that the Revolutionary leaders' professed fears of 'slavery' and of conspiratorial designs were sincere, and drawn from British opposition thought.
c-amrev-bailyn-1967.label: debated
c-amrev-bailyn-1967.note: The 'ideological' interpretation; others put social change (Gordon Wood) or the wider Western world (R. R. Palmer) at the centre.

c-amrev-wood-radicalism.text: In its publisher's words, Gordon Wood's The Radicalism of the American Revolution argues that the Revolution 'transformed an almost feudal society into a democratic one'.
c-amrev-wood-radicalism.label: debated
c-amrev-wood-radicalism.note: Wood's case for a socially radical revolution; Bailyn stressed ideas, Palmer the wider Western setting.

c-amrev-palmer-atlantic.text: R. R. Palmer, in The Age of the Democratic Revolution, treated the American, French and Polish revolutions and other political changes in Europe as, in his publisher's description, manifestations of 'recognizably similar political ideas, needs, and conflicts' across 'the Western world as a whole'.
c-amrev-palmer-atlantic.label: debated
c-amrev-palmer-atlantic.note: An interpretation that treats the American case as one of several connected revolutions rather than as unique.

c-amrev-1619-dispute.text: In the New York Times's words, the passage in question in the 1619 Project's lead essay 'states that one primary reason the colonists fought the American Revolution was to protect the institution of slavery'. Five historians, Wilentz, McPherson, Wood, Bynum and Oakes, read it as asserting that independence was declared to ensure that slavery would continue, and rejected this; the New York Times later clarified that protecting slavery was 'a primary motivation for some of the colonists'.
c-amrev-1619-dispute.label: debated
c-amrev-1619-dispute.note: The five wrote 'This is not true'; Timothy Messer-Kruse argues that the critics misunderstood the project. The Times narrowed its wording but kept the argument.

c-frrev-feudal-abolition-1789.text: By its decree of 11 August 1789, the outcome of the night of 4 August, the National Assembly declared that it 'completely abolishes the feudal system'.
c-frrev-feudal-abolition-1789.label: consensus

c-frrev-rights-of-man-1789.text: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (26 August 1789) declares in its first article that 'Men are born and remain free and equal in rights'; its tenth article says 'No one shall be disquieted on account of his opinions, including his religious views'.
c-frrev-rights-of-man-1789.label: consensus

c-frrev-clermont-tonnerre-1789.text: On 23 December 1789 Count Stanislas de Clermont-Tonnerre told the Assembly: 'We must refuse everything to the Jews as a nation and accord everything to Jews as individuals.'
c-frrev-clermont-tonnerre-1789.label: consensus

c-frrev-jewish-emancipation-1791.text: On 27 September 1791, on a motion by Adrien Duport, the Assembly revoked 'all adjournments, reservations, and exceptions' in earlier decrees 'relative to Jewish individuals', for those who swore the civic oath, which counted as giving up the special privileges Jews had held.
c-frrev-jewish-emancipation-1791.label: consensus

c-frrev-terror-toll.text: During the Terror (5 September 1793 to 27 July 1794) about 17,000 people were officially executed, perhaps 10,000 died in prison or without trial, and at least 300,000 suspects were arrested; it ended with Robespierre's fall on 9 Thermidor (27 July 1794).
c-frrev-terror-toll.label: approx
c-frrev-terror-toll.note: The execution figure goes back to Donald Greer's count (1935); deaths outside the courts are much less certain, hence 'perhaps'.

c-frrev-vendee-toll.text: Estimates of the dead in the war in the Vendée vary widely. Peter McPhee rejects 'Chaunu's ridiculous claim of 500,000 rebel deaths', cites Jean-Clément Martin's estimate of up to 250,000 insurgents and 200,000 republicans, and finds Reynald Secher's own estimate 'far lower, if still massive'. McPhee writes: 'It was not a genocide: huge numbers of people were killed'.
c-frrev-vendee-toll.label: debated
c-frrev-vendee-toll.note: Reynald Secher calls the repression of the Vendée a genocide; McPhee and Martin see a brutal civil war, in which people were not killed for being a distinct Vendéan people.

c-frrev-lefebvre-social.text: Georges Lefebvre's The Coming of the French Revolution (1939) devotes the first four of its six parts to the aristocratic, bourgeois, popular and peasant revolutions; in its publisher's description, 'Georges Lefebvre wrote history "from below"--a Marxist approach.'
c-frrev-lefebvre-social.label: debated
c-frrev-lefebvre-social.note: The 'social' or Marxist interpretation, challenged by the revisionists Alfred Cobban and François Furet.

c-frrev-revisionists.text: Alfred Cobban's The Social Interpretation of the French Revolution (1964) was offered as 'a salutary corrective to many celebrated social explanations', and François Furet's Interpreting the French Revolution (English edition, 1981) distinguished, in its publisher's description, 'between commemorative and conceptual history'.
c-frrev-revisionists.label: debated
c-frrev-revisionists.note: The revisionist challenge to the social interpretation of Lefebvre; the two sides read the same events in different terms.

c-haiti-saint-domingue-1789.text: In 1789 Saint-Domingue held roughly 465,000 (perhaps as many as 500,000) slaves of African descent, about 30,000 whites and a similar number of free people of colour.
c-haiti-saint-domingue-1789.label: approx
c-haiti-saint-domingue-1789.note: The John Carter Brown Library gives a range for the enslaved; the other figures are rounded.

c-haiti-uprising-1791-toussaint.text: In August 1791 thousands of enslaved people in Saint-Domingue rose in rebellion; in May 1801 Toussaint Louverture made himself governor-general for life; seized by the French, he died on 7 April 1803.
c-haiti-uprising-1791-toussaint.label: consensus

c-haiti-french-abolition-1794.text: On 4 February 1794 the National Convention declared 'the abolition of Negro slavery in all the colonies'.
c-haiti-french-abolition-1794.label: consensus

c-haiti-leclerc-independence-1804.text: The French expedition of 1802 under Leclerc, about 40,000 sailors and soldiers, was ruined by fighting and yellow fever; Dessalines defeated the French at Vertières on 18 November 1803, after which Rochambeau surrendered Cap-Français, the last significant French stronghold. Dessalines formally declared Haiti's independence on 1 January 1804, and the French failure contributed to the Louisiana Purchase.
c-haiti-leclerc-independence-1804.label: consensus

c-haiti-1804-killings.text: Philippe Girard writes that 'Blacks won the war and eradicated Haiti's white population in 1804', describes the killings as genocide, and asks that they be read in a specific, Haitian context.
c-haiti-1804-killings.label: debated
c-haiti-1804-killings.note: The label is Girard's own; the title of his article calls the war of 1802-04 a racial war.

c-haiti-indemnity-1825.text: In 1825 Haiti was charged an indemnity of '150 million francs, to be paid in five annual instalments', which President Jean-Pierre Boyer was forced to accept after a French squadron under the baron de Mackau reached Port-au-Prince on 3 July 1825; it was later 'renegotiated downwards (to 90 million francs)', in 1838, and combined with loans it became a double debt.
c-haiti-indemnity-1825.label: consensus

c-haiti-indemnity-payoff.text: The Bibliothèque nationale de France says the independence debt was 'finally paid off by Haiti in 1878 by way of a loan raised on the French market in 1875'; the New York Times's data for 'The Ransom' agree that 'In 1878, Haiti's government made the last payment on the indemnity', and add that 'The double debt was therefore paid off in 1888'. Britannica says the indemnity was 'to be paid at an annual rate until 1887', the year the payments were scheduled to end.
c-haiti-indemnity-payoff.label: approx
c-haiti-indemnity-payoff.note: The last payment on the indemnity itself (1878) and the end of the loans that financed it (1888) are different dates; Britannica's 1887 is the scheduled end of the payments, not the date they stopped.

c-haiti-ransom-nyt-2022.text: The New York Times series 'The Ransom' (2022) estimated that Haiti paid about $560 million in today's dollars, and that the payments cost its economy at least $21 billion, and perhaps as much as $115 billion, in lost growth.
c-haiti-ransom-nyt-2022.label: debated
c-haiti-ransom-nyt-2022.note: The Times's own estimate, reported here through the Equal Justice Initiative's summary; the CEPR authors give a lower central range and a far wider spread of scenarios (see the CEPR paper on this page).

c-haiti-debt-cepr-2021.text: Two economists, Kim Oosterlinck and Ugo Panizza, and two law professors, Mark Weidemaier and Mitu Gulati (2021), put Haiti's initial debt at 'nearly 280%' of GDP and write that 'Our back of the envelope calculations suggest that this cost is large, somewhere between $3 billion and $50 billion'; their table of scenarios runs from $1.6 billion (the gold value) to $1.1 trillion. On one argument, they write, their discussion 'overstates the costs of the French debt'; but if the debt helped produce the kleptocratic regimes that stunted Haiti's development, 'the calculations reported above would understate the real cost of the 1825 debt'.
c-haiti-debt-cepr-2021.label: debated
c-haiti-debt-cepr-2021.note: The spread of the scenarios reflects different assumptions, which the authors set out; their central range is $3-50 billion.

c-haiti-ransom-critique.text: Some critics, such as Yassmin Abdel-Magied, said the Times series was 'telling me much of what I already knew'.
c-haiti-ransom-critique.label: debated
c-haiti-ransom-critique.note: One critic's view, in an opinion column.

c-haiti-macron-2025.text: On 17 April 2025 President Macron said that the 1825 decision 'plaçait alors un prix sur la liberté' (placed a price on freedom) and created 'une commission mixte franco-haïtienne' of historians to examine the shared past; he did not offer reparations.
c-haiti-macron-2025.label: consensus

c-british-abolition-1807-1833.text: Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807. The Abolition of Slavery Act of 1833 came into effect on 1 August 1834, with a period of apprenticeship that ended in 1838, and with 'the grant of £20 million in compensation, to be paid by the British taxpayers to slave owners'.
c-british-abolition-1807-1833.label: consensus

c-williams-thesis-1944.text: Eric Williams (1944) argued that the profits of slavery helped finance British industrialization and that abolition followed the slave economy's decline; in Williams's words, quoted by David Brion Davis, 'Overproduction in 1807 demanded abolition [of the slave trade]'.
c-williams-thesis-1944.label: debated
c-williams-thesis-1944.note: Williams's thesis has two halves, about profits and about abolition; critics such as Seymour Drescher reject the second.

c-drescher-econocide-1977.text: Seymour Drescher (1977) argued that abolition 'resulted not from the diminishing value of slavery' and 'was detrimental to Britain's economic interests'.
c-drescher-econocide-1977.label: debated
c-drescher-econocide-1977.note: Drescher's 'econocide' directly rejects the second half of Williams's thesis.

c-hrv-slavery-wealth-2022.text: Stephan Heblich, Stephen Redding and Hans-Joachim Voth (2022) find that 'slavery wealth raises aggregate income by the equivalent of around a decade of economic growth'.
c-hrv-slavery-wealth-2022.label: debated
c-hrv-slavery-wealth-2022.note: A working paper that revives the first half of Williams's thesis; it is compatible with Drescher's case about abolition, which concerns the second.

c-latam-code.text: On 21 March 1804 France's civil statutes were consolidated in a single body of law, the Civil Code, later known as the Napoleonic Code. It extinguished primogeniture, hereditary nobility and class privileges, but it subordinated women to their fathers and husbands.
c-latam-code.label: consensus

c-latam-code-adopt.text: The Code was voluntarily adopted in a number of European and Latin American countries.
c-latam-code-adopt.label: consensus

c-latam-bayonne.text: In 1808 Napoleon induced the Spanish king Charles IV and his son Ferdinand VII to come to Bayonne. The people of Madrid had already risen against the invader on 2 May; on 5 May Napoleon forced Ferdinand to abdicate in favour of Charles, and Charles in favour of Napoleon himself, who chose his brother Joseph Bonaparte to rule Spain.
c-latam-bayonne.label: consensus

c-latam-cadiz.text: In 1812 Spaniards free of French rule adopted the Constitution of Cádiz, which Britannica calls the 'sacred codex' of Latin liberalism. It proclaimed Spain's American possessions full members of the kingdom and not mere colonies, yet the Creoles who took part in the new Cortes were denied equal representation.
c-latam-cadiz.label: consensus

c-latam-1814.text: When Ferdinand VII returned to Spain in 1814, reactionaries urged him to abolish the Cortes of Cádiz and all its works, and he did so almost immediately.
c-latam-1814.label: consensus

c-latam-hidalgo.text: On 16 September 1810 Miguel Hidalgo called for revolt at Dolores, in New Spain (Mexico), and raised a large popular army. He was executed on 30 July 1811.
c-latam-hidalgo.label: consensus

c-latam-morelos.text: José María Morelos called the Congress of Chilpancingo in 1813 to form a government and draft a constitution, and in November the congress declared Mexico's independence. Morelos was captured, defrocked and shot as a traitor; Britannica gives the date of his death as 22 December 1815.
c-latam-morelos.label: consensus

c-latam-chacabuco.text: José de San Martín led about 5,000 troops on a difficult 20-day march over the high Andes and defeated the Spanish at Chacabuco on 12 February 1817; the expulsion of the Spanish from Chile was completed the next year at the Battle of Maipú.
c-latam-chacabuco.label: approx
c-latam-chacabuco.note: The dates are secure; the size of the army is Britannica's round figure.

c-latam-boyaca.text: Simón Bolívar's victory at Boyacá on 7 August 1819 freed New Granada (Colombia) from Spanish control; he captured Bogotá on 10 August.
c-latam-boyaca.label: consensus

c-latam-ayacucho.text: At Ayacucho on 9 December 1824 an army under Antonio José de Sucre, Bolívar's lieutenant, won a victory that freed Peru and ensured the independence of the new South American republics from Spain.
c-latam-ayacucho.label: consensus

c-latam-loss.text: Between 1808 and 1826 all of Latin America except the Spanish colonies of Cuba and Puerto Rico slipped out of the hands of Spain and Portugal.
c-latam-loss.label: consensus

c-latam-brazil.text: The Portuguese court arrived at Rio de Janeiro on 7 March 1808. On 7 September 1822, on the plain of Ipiranga near São Paulo, Pedro proclaimed the independence of Brazil, and on 1 December he was crowned emperor.
c-latam-brazil.label: consensus

c-latam-lost.text: Robert Bates, John Coatsworth and Jeffrey Williamson (2007) argue that in Latin America, most of which was independent by the 1820s, as in Africa, most of which was independent by 1960, 'independence was followed by political instability, violent conflict, and economic stagnation' for about half a century.
c-latam-lost.label: debated
c-latam-lost.note: Their 'lost decades' view is challenged by Leandro Prados de la Escosura, who finds that per capita income grew after independence.

c-latam-prados.text: Leandro Prados de la Escosura finds that after independence per capita income grew; that Latin America fell behind the US and Western Europe but improved or kept its position relative to the rest of the world; that relief from the colonial fiscal burden was partly offset by the higher costs of self-government; and that emancipation widened regional disparities. He concludes that the label 'lost decades' 'seems an unwarranted depiction of the period 1820-1870'.
c-latam-prados.label: debated
c-latam-prados.note: A working paper (2007) answering the 'lost decades' view of Bates, Coatsworth and Williamson.

c-ir-start.text: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the 18th century; Arnold Toynbee used the term to describe Britain's economic development from 1760 to 1840.
c-ir-start.label: consensus

c-ir-watt.text: On 5 January 1769 the Scottish engineer James Watt was granted a patent for his separate condenser, which vastly improved the efficiency of the steam engine.
c-ir-watt.label: consensus

c-ir-growth.text: As tabulated by Antràs and Voth (2003, Table 1), estimates of annual output growth in England are 1.1% for 1760-1800 and 2.7% for 1801-31 (Feinstein, 1981); 1% and 2% (Crafts, 1985); and 1% for 1760-1801 and 1.9% for 1801-31 (Crafts and Harley, 1992). All three put growth in 1831-60 at 2.5%.
c-ir-growth.label: approx
c-ir-growth.note: Reconstructed estimates for a period without national accounts; Antràs and Voth call the Crafts-Harley rates 'modest'.

c-ir-gradual.text: The Crafts-Harley revisions made the Industrial Revolution look 'a more gradual process than previously believed', but Crafts and Harley still describe it as 'an important discontinuity'.
c-ir-gradual.label: debated
c-ir-gradual.note: Their 1992 article revises their own earlier indices with new data and reasserts 'the idea of the industrial revolution as an important discontinuity'; VoxEU summarises the revisions as making it look more gradual.

c-ir-allen.text: Robert Allen (2009) argues that in Britain 'wages were high and capital and energy cheap in comparison to other countries in Europe and Asia', so that the breakthrough technologies of the Industrial Revolution were uniquely profitable to invent and use there.
c-ir-allen.label: debated
c-ir-allen.note: Allen's 'high-wage economy' thesis. Humphries and Schneider (2019) and Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2023) dispute it from different evidence; Allen restated it in 2015 in reply to Humphries.

c-ir-allen-2015.text: Answering a critique by Jane Humphries, Robert Allen (2015) restated his thesis: 'New evidence is presented to show that women and children participated in the high wage economy.'
c-ir-allen-2015.label: debated
c-ir-allen-2015.note: Allen's reply to Humphries's earlier critique; Humphries and Schneider's study of spinning (2019) came later.

c-ir-humphries.text: Jane Humphries and Benjamin Schneider (2019) find no 'high wage economy' in spinning, 'a leading sector of industrialization': it was 'a widespread, low-productivity, low-wage employment, in which wages did not rise substantially' before the jenny and the water frame. 'The motivation for mechanization must be sought elsewhere.'
c-ir-humphries.label: debated
c-ir-humphries.note: A direct challenge to Allen's thesis, for one leading sector.

c-ir-griffin.text: Reviewing Allen, the historian Emma Griffin writes that 'Allen has convincingly argued that the combination of high wages and cheap fuel deserves a central place in our analyses', but calls the British industrial revolution 'a very large, complex and untidy event, not amenable to any single explanation'.
c-ir-griffin.label: debated
c-ir-griffin.note: One reviewer's judgement: broadly favourable to Allen, but doubtful of any single cause.

c-ir-kmo.text: Testing competing explanations across English counties from the 1760s to the 1830s, Morgan Kelly, Joel Mokyr and Cormac Ó Gráda (2023) find that 'industrialization occurred in areas that began with low wages but high mechanical skills', while literacy, banks and proximity to coal have 'little explanatory power'.
c-ir-kmo.label: debated
c-ir-kmo.note: New econometric work; its emphasis on low wages and mechanical skill runs against Allen's high-wage, cheap-energy thesis.

c-ir-feinstein.text: Charles Feinstein (1998), adjusting workers' real earnings for unemployment, dependants and the costs of urbanization, found that the standard of living of the average working-class family 'improved by less than 15 percent between the 1780s and 1850s'.
c-ir-feinstein.label: debated
c-ir-feinstein.note: The 'pessimist' side of the standard-of-living debate. Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2023) stress instead how wages differed by region.

c-ir-regional.text: Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda (2023) find that 'real wages rose sharply in the industrializing north and declined in the previously prosperous south'.
c-ir-regional.label: debated
c-ir-regional.note: They present this against the view that living standards stagnated, the view associated with Feinstein.

c-ir-pomeranz.text: Kenneth Pomeranz argues that Britain 'was able to overcome its land constraint by substituting wood with coal' and by 'importing foodstuffs and raw cotton from the Americas'. Writing with Prasannan Parthasarathi, he says the claim that England and the Yangzi delta were roughly at parity in living standards in 1750 'remains plausible, though disputed', while the same claim for 1800 is less so.
c-ir-pomeranz.label: debated
c-ir-pomeranz.note: The 'California School' view, set out in Pomeranz's The Great Divergence (2000). Broadberry, Guan and Li (2018) date the divergence earlier.

c-ir-bgl.text: Using historical national accounts, Stephen Broadberry, Hanhui Guan and David Daokui Li (2018) conclude that the Great Divergence between Europe and China began 'earlier than originally suggested by the California School' but 'later than implied by older Eurocentric writers'.
c-ir-bgl.label: debated
c-ir-bgl.note: Their GDP estimates for China, back to 980, place the divergence between the two older camps.

c-ind-rail.text: The Stockton and Darlington, a steam-hauled public railway, opened on 27 September 1825; the Liverpool and Manchester, the world's first inter-city line, followed in 1830.
c-ind-rail.label: consensus

c-ind-belgium.text: Belgium, which was developing machine shops at Liège around 1807, became the first country in continental Europe to be transformed economically; in 1835 a train ran from Brussels to Mechelen.
c-ind-belgium.label: consensus

c-ind-germany-us.text: Britannica says that France industrialized more slowly and less thoroughly than Britain or Belgium, that Germany did not begin its industrial expansion until after national unity was achieved in 1870, and that the rise of US industrial power in the 19th and 20th centuries far outstripped European efforts. John Munro, by contrast, writes of Germany that 'From the 1850s, there is much more rapid growth and discernible industrialization', 'so that we might talk of a "take-off"'.
c-ind-germany-us.label: debated
c-ind-germany-us.note: The dating of German industrialization is disputed: Britannica places its start after unification, Munro's lecture notes a 'take-off' in the 1850s. When a country's industrialization 'began' depends on what is measured.

c-ind-tomioka.text: Early in the Meiji period the Japanese government founded the Tomioka silk mill (1872) with imported French machinery and industrial expertise; at the beginning of the 20th century Japan became the world's leading exporter of raw silk, notably to Europe and the United States.
c-ind-tomioka.label: consensus

c-ind-factoryact.text: Britain's Factory Act of 1833 barred children under nine from factories, limited children aged 9 to 13 to 48 hours a week and eight hours a day and those aged 13 to 18 to 12 hours a day, required children under 13 to receive two hours of schooling a day, and created a four-man inspectorate of factories. Earlier acts had applied only to the cotton industry; this one also covered the woollen districts around Yorkshire.
c-ind-factoryact.label: consensus

c-ind-manifesto.text: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels's Manifesto of the Communist Party was first published in February 1848. It opens, in Samuel Moore's translation of 1888: 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.'
c-ind-manifesto.label: consensus

c-ind-1848.text: The revolutions of 1848, republican revolts against European monarchies, began with a local revolution in Sicily in January. After the revolution of 24 February in France they spread throughout Europe except Russia, Spain and the Scandinavian countries. Britannica judges that 'They all ended in failure and repression'; yet some reforms lasted. In Austria the revolutionary Reichstag 'fully emancipated the peasantry', and 'The conservative regime that followed kept and implemented this law'; in Denmark, after the demonstrations of March 1848, Frederick VII 'renounced absolute rule and adopted a representative government'.
c-ind-1848.label: debated
c-ind-1848.note: Britannica's verdict of failure concerns the revolutionaries' immediate aims; some reforms of 1848 outlasted the reaction.

c-ind-bismarck.text: Bismarck's Germany introduced sickness insurance (1883), workers' compensation (1884) and, in 1889, the world's first old-age social insurance programme, with a retirement age of 70, lowered to 65 in 1916.
c-ind-bismarck.label: consensus

c-ind-motives.text: According to the US Social Security Administration's history, Bismarck acted both to promote the well-being of workers, in order to keep the German economy operating at maximum efficiency, and 'to stave-off calls for more radical socialist alternatives'. Called a socialist for it, he replied: 'Call it socialism or whatever you like. It is the same to me.'
c-ind-motives.label: debated
c-ind-motives.note: The SSA's account names both motives, welfare and efficiency on one side and heading off socialism on the other; how to weigh them is a matter of interpretation.

c-nat-italy.text: The Kingdom of Italy was established in 1861; Venetia was annexed in 1866 and papal Rome in 1870.
c-nat-italy.label: consensus

c-nat-germany.text: The German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles on 18 January 1871, with Wilhelm as emperor.
c-nat-germany.label: consensus

c-nat-gellner.text: At Warwick on 24 October 1995 Ernest Gellner, who held that nations are modern, debated Anthony Smith, who stressed their ethnic roots. Gellner said that 'the world was created round about the end of the eighteenth century'; of ethnic continuity he said 'Some nations have it and some don't and in any case it's inessential'; and of Smith, 'He says modernism only tells half the story.'
c-nat-gellner.label: debated
c-nat-gellner.note: Gellner's modernism against Smith's emphasis on the ethnic roots of nations; the exchange is recorded on the LSE's Gellner pages.

c-nat-anderson.text: Benedict Anderson called the nation an 'imagined' community, 'imagined because the members of even the smallest nation will never know most of their fellow-members'.
c-nat-anderson.label: debated
c-nat-anderson.note: That this is Anderson's definition is not in doubt; how far it explains nationalism is debated.

c-nat-hobsbawm.text: Eric Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger (1983) argued that many traditions thought to be ancient 'were invented comparatively recently'.
c-nat-hobsbawm.label: debated
c-nat-hobsbawm.note: A modernist argument, in the same camp as Gellner; scholars such as Anthony Smith emphasise older ethnic continuities.

c-nat-marr.text: Wilhelm Marr is credited with coining the term 'antisemitism' in the 1870s; his tract The Victory of Judaism over Germandom (1879) ran through twelve editions in its first year. 'Racial antisemitism dates to the late 19th century.'
c-nat-marr.label: approx
c-nat-marr.note: German History in Documents says Marr is 'most famous for coining the term'; the first use of a word is hard to prove.

c-nat-pogroms.text: The first pogrom in the Russian empire's wave of 1881 occurred at Yelizavetgrad (now Kropyvnytskyi), in Ukraine, at the end of April 1881; restrictive laws followed, among them the May Laws of 1882.
c-nat-pogroms.label: consensus

c-nat-kishinev.text: At Kishinev, during Passover 1903, a pogrom followed agitation by the local antisemitic newspaper Bessarabets; the Encyclopaedia Judaica counts '45 dead and hundreds of wounded', while the publisher's description of Steven Zipperstein's study says that 'In three days of violence, 49 Jews were killed and 600 raped or wounded.'
c-nat-kishinev.label: approx
c-nat-kishinev.note: Counts of the dead differ: 45 in the Encyclopaedia Judaica (via the Jewish Virtual Library), 49 in the description of Zipperstein's book.

c-nat-dreyfus.text: The army captain Alfred Dreyfus, who was Jewish, was convicted of treason in December 1894 for allegedly selling military secrets to the Germans. Much of the early publicity came from antisemitic groups. Émile Zola's letter 'J'accuse' appeared in Clemenceau's newspaper L'Aurore; in July 1906 a civilian appeals court set aside the judgment, but the army did not publicly declare his innocence until 1995.
c-nat-dreyfus.label: consensus

c-nat-herzl.text: Theodor Herzl's The Jewish State appeared in 1896. Its preface begins: 'The idea which I have developed in this pamphlet is a very old one: it is the restoration of the Jewish State.' He wrote that 'The Jewish question exists wherever Jews live in perceptible numbers.'
c-nat-herzl.label: consensus

c-nat-herzl-dreyfus.text: Did the Dreyfus affair make Herzl a Zionist? Herzl could say later that it had. Shlomo Avineri calls this 'simply not true': 'It was not the trial of Alfred Dreyfus, but Herzl's long analysis of the failure of emancipation and the rise of German and Austrian anti-Semitism.'
c-nat-herzl-dreyfus.label: debated
c-nat-herzl-dreyfus.note: Herzl's own later account against Avineri's reading of his writings.

c-nat-basel.text: The First Zionist Congress opened in the concert hall of the Basel Municipal Casino on 29 August 1897. About 200 people from seventeen countries attended, 69 of them delegates. Its programme began, in one translation: 'Zionism seeks to establish a home for the Jewish people in Eretz-Israel secured under public law'; Britannica renders the goal as 'a home in Palestine secured by public law'.
c-nat-basel.label: approx
c-nat-basel.note: The Jewish Virtual Library notes 'some dispute as to the exact number' attending.

c-nat-zionism-meaning.text: Zionism's meaning is contested. Britannica notes that in the years of the British Mandate 'the Arab population feared that Palestine would eventually become a Jewish state'. The description of Derek Penslar's study (2023) says that 'For those who identify as Zionist, the word connotes liberation and redemption', while for others it is 'a source of distaste if not disgust', and offers 'a new take on its relationship to colonialism'.
c-nat-zionism-meaning.label: debated
c-nat-zionism-meaning.note: Penslar's book examines both responses and the movement's relationship to colonialism. See 14.12.

c-eman-russia.text: By Alexander II's Emancipation Manifesto of 3 March 1861 (19 February, Old Style), Russia's serfs were freed. They were organized in village communities and were to repay the exchequer over 49 years for the land they received.
c-eman-russia.label: consensus

c-eman-share.text: The emancipation 'liberated roughly 40 percent of the population from bondage', but the Great Reforms of which it was part 'did not alter the political structure of the empire'.
c-eman-share.label: approx

c-eman-13th.text: In 1863 President Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation, but it did not end slavery in the nation. The Thirteenth Amendment, passed by Congress at the end of the Civil War on 31 January 1865 and ratified on 6 December 1865, declares: 'Neither slavery nor involuntary servitude, except as a punishment for crime whereof the party shall have been duly convicted, shall exist within the United States, or any place subject to their jurisdiction.'
c-eman-13th.label: consensus

c-eman-1877.text: The Compromise of 1877 was an unwritten deal that settled the disputed presidential election of 1876, in which Samuel Tilden outpolled Rutherford B. Hayes by 250,000 votes but the Electoral College decided the winner. It secured the White House for Hayes; federal troops were removed from Florida, Louisiana and South Carolina, effectively ending Reconstruction in those states.
c-eman-1877.label: approx
c-eman-1877.note: Whether a bargain was actually struck is debated; see Allan Peskin, 'Was There a Compromise of 1877?', Journal of American History 60:1 (1973), doi:10.2307/2936329. The withdrawal of the troops is not in dispute.

c-eman-cuba.text: In Cuba a law of 13 February 1880 replaced slavery with the patronato and set a limit of eight years for the final suppression of the slave system; a Royal Decree of 7 October 1886 ended the patronato two years before that deadline.
c-eman-cuba.label: consensus

c-eman-brazil.text: Brazil decreed complete emancipation, without compensation to the owners, on 13 May 1888.
c-eman-brazil.label: consensus

c-eman-fogel.text: Robert Fogel's work of 1974 with Stanley Engerman, Time on the Cross, argued that American slavery, 'in spite of its inhumanity, had been economically efficient', and that it collapsed because of political decisions, not economic weakness. It 'aroused great attention and bitter controversies'.
c-eman-fogel.label: debated
c-eman-fogel.note: Fogel shared the 1993 Nobel prize in economics. Critics, as Peter Coclanis puts it, 'attacked from several different directions'.

c-eman-critics.text: Fogel and Engerman's critics 'attacked from several different directions', notably Herbert Gutman's Slavery and the Numbers Game (1975) and Paul David and others' Reckoning with Slavery (1976).
c-eman-critics.label: debated
c-eman-critics.note: Peter Coclanis's summary of the controversy.

c-eman-nhc.text: The 'new history of capitalism', in books by Sven Beckert, Walter Johnson and Edward Baptist, 'grounds the rise of industrial capitalism on the production of raw cotton by American slaves'. Alan Olmstead and Paul Rhode (2018) reply that 'All three authors mishandle historical evidence and mis-characterize important events'.
c-eman-nhc.label: debated
c-eman-nhc.note: Olmstead and Rhode say the errors affect these authors' accounts of slavery, plantations, cotton's place in the wider economy and the sources of the Industrial Revolution.

c-qing-opium-wars.text: Foreign traders, mainly British, had been illegally exporting opium, mainly from India, to China since the 18th century. After the Chinese government confiscated and destroyed more than 20,000 chests of opium at Canton, Britain and China fought the first Opium War (1839-42); Britain and France fought China in the second (1856-60).
c-qing-opium-wars.label: consensus

c-qing-nanjing.text: The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) required China to pay Britain a large indemnity, to cede Hong Kong Island to the British, and to increase the treaty ports where the British could trade and reside from one (Canton) to five.
c-qing-nanjing.label: consensus

c-qing-1860.text: In 1858 the importation of opium was legalized; in 1860 British and French troops captured Beijing and plundered and then burned the Yuanming Garden, the emperor's summer palace.
c-qing-1860.label: consensus

c-qing-hong.text: The Taiping rebellion (1850-64) was led by Hong Xiuquan, a disappointed civil-service examination candidate who believed himself to be the son of God, the younger brother of Jesus Christ. The Taipings took Nanjing on 10 March 1853 and renamed it Tianjing ('Heavenly Capital'); the city fell in July 1864.
c-qing-hong.label: consensus

c-qing-taiping-suppress.text: Forces organised under Zeng Guofan, a Qing official, fought the Taipings, as did the Western-trained 'Ever-Victorious Army', commanded by the American Frederick Townsend Ward and later by the British officer Charles George Gordon.
c-qing-taiping-suppress.label: consensus

c-qing-taiping-toll.text: The Taiping rebellion's death toll is given as an estimated 20 million (Britannica) or some 30 million (an interview page on Tobie Meyer-Fong's book What Remains); a popular history says conservative estimates start at between 20 and 30 million and that much of the mortality has been attributed to disease and famine rather than military conflict.
c-qing-taiping-toll.label: approx
c-qing-taiping-toll.note: Round estimates, not counts. All About History is a popular magazine; it gives no single total.

c-qing-selfstr.text: In the Self-Strengthening Movement (1861-95), Zeng Guofan, Li Hongzhang and Zuo Zongtang sought to consolidate Qing power by introducing Western technology; Britannica notes 'some notable gains' but judges that its overall success was 'limited'.
c-qing-selfstr.label: debated
c-qing-selfstr.note: An assessment, not a measurement: Britannica weighs the movement's gains against its overall result.

c-qing-meiji.text: The Meiji Restoration brought about the fall of the Tokugawa shogunate and returned Japan to direct imperial rule under the emperor Meiji; the Meiji period ran from 1868 to 1912.
c-qing-meiji.label: consensus

c-qing-meiji-reforms.text: In 1871 Japan's new government declared feudalism abolished, and nearly 300 fiefs became 72 prefectures and 3 metropolitan districts; in 1873 it instituted nationwide conscription and set a land tax of 3 percent of the land's assessed value.
c-qing-meiji-reforms.label: consensus

c-qing-sinojap.text: The Sino-Japanese War, declared on 1 August 1894, grew out of conflict between China and Japan for supremacy in Korea. By the peace of 1895 (the Treaty of Shimonoseki) China recognized the independence of Korea, ceded Taiwan, the Pescadores and the Liaodong Peninsula in Manchuria, and agreed to pay a large indemnity, but Russia, France and Germany together forced Japan to return the Liaodong Peninsula to China.
c-qing-sinojap.label: consensus

c-qing-portarthur.text: In 1898 Russia pressured China into granting it a lease of Port Arthur (now Lüshun), at the tip of the Liaodong Peninsula in southern Manchuria.
c-qing-portarthur.label: consensus

c-qing-boxer-rising.text: In 1900 the Boxers (Yihequan, 'Righteous and Harmonious Fists'), a secret society encouraged by the empress dowager Cixi, attacked Chinese Christians and Western missionaries and besieged foreign diplomats and Chinese Christians in the legation quarter and the Catholic cathedral in Beijing; an international force of some 19,000 troops took Beijing on 14 August 1900.
c-qing-boxer-rising.label: consensus

c-qing-boxer.text: The Boxer Protocol, signed at Peking on 7 September 1901, imposed an indemnity of 450,000,000 Haikwan taels, bearing interest at 4 percent a year, to be paid off by the end of 1940.
c-qing-boxer.label: consensus

c-qing-russojap.text: The Russo-Japanese War (1904-05) arose from rivalry between Russia and Japan for dominance in Korea and Manchuria; Japan's victory made it 'the first Asian power in modern times to defeat a European power'.
c-qing-russojap.label: consensus

c-raj-1857.text: The rebellion of 1857-58, an unsuccessful rising against British rule in India, began among the Indian troops (sepoys) of the British East India Company at Meerut and spread to Delhi, Agra, Kanpur and Lucknow.
c-raj-1857.label: consensus

c-raj-1857-causes.text: What to call the rising is itself contested: Britannica's article is titled 'Indian Mutiny', but in India it is often called the First War of Independence, and Britannica warns that 'To regard the rebellion merely as a sepoy mutiny is to underestimate the root causes leading to it', linking it to British paramountcy in Indian political, economic and cultural life.
c-raj-1857-causes.label: debated
c-raj-1857-causes.note: The two names reflect two readings: a military mutiny, or a wider revolt against British rule.

c-raj-crown.text: On 2 August 1858 Parliament transferred British power over India from the East India Company to the Crown, and the Company was abolished; the British raj, the period of direct British rule, lasted until 1947. In 1876 Queen Victoria added the title Empress of India.
c-raj-crown.label: consensus

c-raj-famine.text: In the famine of 1876-78 an estimated 5.5 million people in South and Southwestern India died of starvation; the V&A's catalogue, following Mike Davis, attributes the famine to drought but adds that 'the commodification and export of grain by the colonial government also played a key role'.
c-raj-famine.label: debated
c-raj-famine.note: The figure and the emphasis on policy are Davis's (Late Victorian Holocausts, 2001). Tirthankar Roy gives the main role to geography and the monsoon.

c-raj-lytton.text: In autumn 1876, as crops failed in southern India, the viceroy, Lord Lytton, was organising the Imperial Assemblage at Delhi, which proclaimed Victoria Empress of India and included 'a week-long feast for 68,000 officials, satraps and maharajas'. In 1877 Lytton told the Legislative Council that India's population 'has a tendency to increase more rapidly than the food it raises from the soil'.
c-raj-lytton.label: debated
c-raj-lytton.note: From Mike Davis's account, as quoted in the V&A's catalogue; setting the feast beside the famine is Davis's argument.

c-raj-sh.text: Dylan Sullivan and Jason Hickel (2023) write that measured against England's 16th- and 17th-century average death rate, 'we find 165 million excess deaths in India between 1880 and 1920'; taking India's own average death rate of the 1880s as normal mortality, they find some 50 million excess deaths for 1891-1920.
c-raj-sh.label: debated
c-raj-sh.note: New and contested. The total depends on what counts as 'normal' mortality: Sullivan and Hickel call the 50 million figure conservative, while Tirthankar Roy rejects colonial rule as the cause of the famines.

c-raj-roy.text: Tirthankar Roy (2023) argues that 'The British Raj did not start the famines. Geography did.' Monsoon rain was the main source of water, and the Deccan was normally much drier than the north ('Why did it spare the north?'); he holds that 'trade stabilized domestic consumption rather than reducing it', that 'statistical research confirms that the railways caused the end of famines', and that state efforts brought 'a sharp fall in death rates from 1901'. In a working paper of 2016 he wrote that 'a mainly geographical account diminishes the role of the state in the occurrence and retreat of famines, whereas a mainly political account overstates that role'.
c-raj-roy.label: debated
c-raj-roy.note: History Reclaimed is an opinion site; the 2016 paper is Roy's scholarly statement. Critics including Jason Hickel and Tamoghna Halder have replied to Roy, blaming colonial policy.

c-raj-drain.text: Jason Hickel reports that Utsa Patnaik (Columbia University Press, 2018) finds that 'the total drain amounts to $44.6 trillion' for 1765-1938, with interest compounded to the present at 'about 5 percent, which is lower than the market rate'; Tirthankar Roy replies that her claim is 'based on dreadfully bad economics and is still untestable'.
c-raj-drain.label: debated
c-raj-drain.note: Patnaik and Hickel against Roy. Roy rounds the figure to 45 trillion dollars.

c-raj-dh.text: Lance Davis and Robert Huttenback (1982) found the empire 'relatively very profitable in the years before 1880', but domestic investment paid better from about 1880, and empire returns were high 'only because of substantial social subsidies from the British'; they write that 'The imperial experience could therefore be viewed more as a redistribution of income within the United Kingdom than as a transfer from the empire to the mother country.' Their book concludes that 'returns from empire investment were not high in comparison to earnings in the domestic and foreign sectors' and that 'empire profits were earned at a substantial cost to the taxpayer', in 'an income transfer from the tax-paying middle class to the elites'.
c-raj-dh.label: debated
c-raj-dh.note: Davis and Huttenback measure returns to British investors and costs to British taxpayers; Patnaik measures transfers out of India. The two estimates answer different questions.

c-raj-berlin.text: The Berlin West Africa Conference (15 November 1884 to 26 February 1885), proposed by Portugal, dealt with questions connected with the Congo River basin; its act guaranteed freedom for trade and shipping for all states in the basin and forbade slave trading.
c-raj-berlin.label: consensus

c-raj-congo.text: The Congo Free State (1885-1908) was the private holding of a group of European investors headed by Leopold II, under his 'unrestrained personal control'. Forced labour was used to gather wild rubber, palm oil and ivory, and Force Publique troops cut off the hands of Congolese, including children. After a campaign by the Congo Reform Association, founded by British citizens, the state was abolished in 1908 and replaced by the Belgian Congo, controlled by the Belgian parliament.
c-raj-congo.label: consensus

c-raj-boma.text: Boma, on the Congo River estuary, became the capital of the Congo Free State in 1886.
c-raj-boma.label: consensus

c-raj-congo-pop.text: The population of the Congo Free State 'is said to have declined from some 20 million to 8 million'.
c-raj-congo-pop.label: approx
c-raj-congo-pop.note: Britannica's 'is said to' marks a reported estimate, not a count.

c-raj-herero.text: In South West Africa (today's Namibia), German forces defeated the Herero at the Waterberg on 11-12 August 1904; the survivors were deliberately driven into the waterless Omaheke sandveld, where thousands died of thirst. General Lothar von Trotha called for the extermination of the population, and most historians today call the war he led a genocide.
c-raj-herero.label: consensus

c-raj-herero-toll.text: Historians estimate that about 65,000 Herero and at least 10,000 Nama were killed in 1904-08 (AP); the German Historical Museum gives 35-80 percent of some 40,000-100,000 Herero and up to half of about 22,000 Nama. About 1,750 Germans died in the war.
c-raj-herero-toll.label: approx
c-raj-herero-toll.note: The pre-war populations themselves are uncertain, hence the wide ranges; RNZ reports that 'up to 80 percent of the indigenous populations died'.

c-raj-2021.text: In 2021 Germany's foreign minister, Heiko Maas, said: 'We will now officially call these events what they were from today's perspective: a genocide.' Germany offered 1.1 billion euros, largely for development projects over 30 years, but said that 'legal claims to compensation cannot be derived from this'.
c-raj-2021.label: consensus

c-raj-2025.text: Some descendants rejected the offer: Laidlaw Peringanda of the Namibian Genocide Association said, 'We're actually not accepting that offer because our people have lost lands, they have lost their culture.' Namibia observed its first genocide remembrance day on 28 May 2025, when the president said the government would continue to push for reparations from Germany.
c-raj-2025.label: debated
c-raj-2025.note: Germany treats its payment as aid without legal liability; Herero and Nama groups and Namibia's government press for reparations, and descendants want Germany to negotiate with them directly.

c-ott-muhammadali.text: Muhammad Ali, named the Ottoman sultan's viceroy in Egypt in 1805, had converted most of Egypt's agricultural land into state land by 1815, introduced new crops such as cotton, which promised high cash returns, and created a fleet and an army of Egyptians conscripted from the peasant class. 'His industrial experiments failed, largely because Egypt lacked sources of power.' Rule passed to his son Ibrahim in 1848, and he died in 1849.
c-ott-muhammadali.label: consensus

c-ott-tanzimat.text: The Tanzimat was a series of reforms promulgated in the Ottoman Empire between 1839 and 1876. The Hatt-ı Şerif of Gülhane (1839) promised 'security of life, property, and honour to all subjects of the empire', a standardized system of taxation and fairer conscription, but the promises of equality for non-Muslims (mainly Christians and Jews) 'were not always carried out'.
c-ott-tanzimat.label: consensus

c-ott-1876.text: Abdülhamid II promulgated the first Ottoman constitution on 23 December 1876; in February 1878 he suspended it and dismissed the parliament, which had met in March 1877.
c-ott-1876.label: consensus

c-ott-youngturk.text: The Young Turk Revolution (3-23 July 1908), led by members of the III Army Corps in Macedonia, demanded 'the immediate restoration of the 1876 constitution' and restored constitutional government. After a short-lived reactionary uprising in April 1909 Abdülhamid was deposed, and the Committee of Union and Progress took the reins of government in 1913.
c-ott-youngturk.label: consensus

c-ott-iran.text: Iran's Constitutional Revolution began with protests in December 1905; after a sanctuary at the British legation in July 1906, the shah's decree of 5 August 1906 was followed by the constitution adopted on 27 December 1906. Mohammad-ʿAli Shah's coup of 23 June 1908 began the 'lesser tyranny' until the constitution was restored on 16 July 1909; after the joint ultimatum of November 1911 and the expulsion of Morgan Shuster, the American financial adviser to the Persian government, the Second Majles was dissolved on 24 December 1911.
c-ott-iran.label: consensus

c-ott-suez.text: Ferdinand de Lesseps obtained a concession from Said Pasha, and the Suez Canal Company came into being in 1858; the canal opened to shipping on 17 November 1869. External debts forced Isma'il Pasha to put Egypt's shares in the company up for sale, and in 1875 N M Rothschild & Sons advanced Benjamin Disraeli, acting for the British government, £4 million to buy them; France remained the majority shareholder.
c-ott-suez.label: consensus

c-ott-egyptdebt.text: Expensive development projects, such as the digging of the Suez Canal, left Egypt deep in debt; it declared bankruptcy in 1876 and accepted British and French control of its revenues, which assigned 60 percent of revenues to debt payment.
c-ott-egyptdebt.label: consensus

c-ott-urabi.text: 'Urabi led a movement to subject Egypt's hereditary Ottoman governor, Khedive Tawfiq, to constitutional rule. After riots in Alexandria in June 1882 the British launched a full-scale invasion to return Tawfiq to power; the battle of Tel al-Kabir was disastrous for the Egyptians, 'Urabi was tried and exiled, and the rebellion provoked the British occupation of Egypt in 1882.
c-ott-urabi.label: consensus

c-ott-aliyah1.text: The First Aliyah, usually dated 1882-1904, brought about 30,000 young Jews from Europe and Yemen to Ottoman Palestine, amid upheaval in Russian Jewry after the pogroms of 1881-82. Among the first colonies were Rishon Lezion, Zichron Yaacov, Rosh Pina and Petah Tikva, which Britannica says was founded in 1878; the most prominent of their benefactors was Baron Edmond James de Rothschild.
c-ott-aliyah1.label: approx
c-ott-aliyah1.note: A round figure from the National Library of Israel.

c-ott-aliyah2.text: The Second Aliyah (1904-14) brought about 35,000 immigrants, mostly from Eastern Europe and a minority from Yemen. Its ideal was 'Hebrew labor', though many farmers kept employing Arab workers; at Passover 1909 a lottery assigned plots in what became Tel Aviv. At least half of the immigrants left within a few years, and at the end of the period the Jewish community numbered about 80,000.
c-ott-aliyah2.label: approx
c-ott-aliyah2.note: Round figures from the National Library of Israel.

c-ott-pop.text: Reviewing Justin McCarthy's adjustments of Ottoman figures, Roger Owen reports about 340,000 people in 1877-78 and 722,143 in 1914-15 in the territory that later became Palestine. The Ottoman count of its Jewish subjects in 1914-15 was 38,754, against a generally accepted figure of 85,000 for all Jews; McCarthy argues that the true number of Ottoman Jews and Jews with foreign citizenship was closer to 60,000, a figure supported by a census the Zionists themselves took during the First World War.
c-ott-pop.label: debated
c-ott-pop.note: Owen notes that Ottoman registers persistently undercounted young children, especially girls. McCarthy's 60,000 is below the National Library of Israel's figure of about 80,000. The review on this site is in Arabic.

c-ott-pop-jvl.text: A Jewish Virtual Library table gives, for 1914, about 525,000 Muslims, 94,000 Jews and 70,000 Christians and others, a total of 689,000, noting that 'Figures are not exact'.
c-ott-pop-jvl.label: approx
c-ott-pop-jvl.note: The table names no source for its 1914 column.

c-ott-minority.text: On every one of these estimates of the Jewish population, Jews were a small minority of Palestine's population in 1914, between about 8 and 14 percent; Jewish Ottoman subjects alone were about 5 percent.
c-ott-minority.label: approx
c-ott-minority.note: Our arithmetic: McCarthy's 60,000 and the accepted 85,000 are 8.3 and 11.8 percent of his 722,143; 94,000 is 13.6 percent of the Jewish Virtual Library's 689,000; the 38,754 Jewish Ottoman subjects are 5.4 percent of 722,143 but are not an estimate of all Jews. The totals and the Jewish figures do not always cover exactly the same people.

c-glob-bang.text: Kevin O'Rourke and Jeffrey Williamson find no evidence that the world economy was globally integrated before 1492 or 1498, but 'abundant evidence supporting the view that the 19th century contained a very big globalization bang'.
c-glob-bang.label: debated
c-glob-bang.note: Their test is the convergence of commodity prices; Flynn and Giráldez, using the flow of silver, date global trade to 1571 (13.6).

c-glob-freight.text: Transport costs fell as steamships and the Suez Canal (completed in November 1869) linked continents and railroads reached into their interiors; the North freight rate index dropped by 'more than 41 percent, in real terms, between 1870 and 1910'.
c-glob-freight.label: consensus

c-glob-wheat.text: Liverpool wheat prices exceeded Chicago prices by 57.6 percent in 1870, by 17.8 percent in 1895 and by 15.6 percent in 1912.
c-glob-wheat.label: approx
c-glob-wheat.note: O'Rourke and Williamson, from Knick Harley's data.

c-glob-cable.text: In July 1866 a telegraph cable joined Ireland and Newfoundland, after several failed attempts beginning in 1857; messages crossed the Atlantic 'in a matter of minutes' rather than in 10 days by ship.
c-glob-cable.label: consensus

c-glob-gold.text: Britain formally adopted the gold standard in 1816 and effectively resumed it in 1821. 'The rush to the gold standard occurred in the 1870s, with the adherence of Germany, the Scandinavian countries, France, and other European countries'; the United States had a dual legal and effective gold standard from 1879. The outbreak of the First World War in August 1914 brought the classical gold standard to an end.
c-glob-gold.label: consensus

c-glob-ranges.text: A world-history textbook table gives long-distance migration in 1846-1940 as 55-58 million from Europe to the Americas; 48-52 million from India and southern China to Southeast Asia, the Indian Ocean rim and the South Pacific; and 46-51 million from Northeast Asia and Russia to Manchuria, Siberia, Central Asia and Japan.
c-glob-ranges.label: approx
c-glob-ranges.note: Rounded ranges. The table does not name its source on the page; the figures match those widely attributed to Adam McKeown, 'Global Migration, 1846-1940', Journal of World History (2004).

c-glob-mckeown.text: Adam McKeown compares the United States and Southeast Asia, 'regions which respectively received 39 and 35 million migrant arrivals from 1870 to 1930', and says that Timothy Hatton and Jeffrey Williamson (2005) make 'the common error of assuming that indentured migration accounts for the bulk of Asian migrations'.
c-glob-mckeown.label: debated
c-glob-mckeown.note: McKeown (2007, 2010) argues against treating Asian migration as mostly coerced; his target is Hatton and Williamson's Global Migration and the World Economy (2005).

c-glob-india-return.text: Prabhu Mohapatra writes that 'while 30 million migrants left the shores of India between 1834 and 1937 no less than 24 million returned during the same period'.
c-glob-india-return.label: approx

c-glob-indenture.text: Between 1834 and 1920 almost half a million indentured labourers arrived from India at the Aapravasi Ghat in Mauritius, the site of what, UNESCO says, the British government called 'the great experiment' in the use of 'free' labour to replace slaves; the last indentured labourers went to the West Indies in 1916.
c-glob-indenture.label: consensus

c-glob-argentina.text: From 1870 to 1914, 5.9 million immigrants arrived in Argentina, and more than half of them settled permanently; most came from Italy and Spain. The foreign-born share of the population rose from 12 percent in 1869 to 30 percent nationwide in 1914 and 50 percent in Buenos Aires.
c-glob-argentina.label: approx
c-glob-argentina.note: Rounded figures reported by the Migration Policy Institute.

c-glob-ba.text: In 1914 almost 30 percent of Argentina's population was foreign-born, against 22 percent in Canada, 17 in Australia and 15 in the United States. Around 1895 Italians and Spaniards were 51 and 23 percent of the immigrants to Buenos Aires; Spaniards earned between seven and ten percent less than Italians, which Leticia Arroyo Abad, Noel Maurer and Blanca Sánchez-Alonso suggest is because 'individualistic Spanish immigrants viewed each other as competitors for the same jobs, not compatriots to be helped'.
c-glob-ba.label: debated
c-glob-ba.note: The wage gap is measured; the explanation, weaker immigrant networks, is the authors' interpretation of their results.

c-glob-diaz.text: Porfirio Díaz, elected president of Mexico in 1877 and again in 1884, encouraged investment by foreigners, who came to build railroads and bridges, dig mines and irrigate fields, but 'most of the profits went abroad or stayed in the hands of a very few wealthy Mexicans'; faced with revolution, his government collapsed, and he resigned on 25 May 1911 and went into exile.
c-glob-diaz.label: consensus

c-thought-lyell.text: Charles Lyell's Principles of Geology (1830-33) explained the earth's features by natural causes, ordinary processes working slowly over long periods, so that the earth must be very ancient; Darwin wrote that his first geological fieldwork 'showed me clearly the wonderful superiority of Lyell's manner of treating geology'.
c-thought-lyell.label: consensus

c-thought-darwin.text: Charles Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) 'has deeply influenced modern Western society and thought'. Darwin 'at first shocked religious Victorian society by suggesting that animals and humans shared a common ancestry', but his nonreligious biology appealed to the rising class of professional scientists.
c-thought-darwin.label: consensus

c-thought-oxford.text: On 30 June 1860, at the Oxford University Museum, Samuel Wilberforce, Bishop of Oxford, and the biologist Thomas Huxley clashed before almost 500 people; 'no-one accurately recorded what was said', but Huxley is claimed to have retorted, 'I unhesitatingly affirm my preference for the ape.'
c-thought-oxford.label: tradition
c-thought-oxford.note: The museum presents Huxley's retort as a claim, not a record.

c-thought-mosaic.text: The books of the Torah were traditionally ascribed to Moses, the recipient of the original revelation from God on Mount Sinai.
c-thought-mosaic.label: tradition
c-thought-mosaic.note: Held by tradition; Wellhausen and later source critics reject Mosaic authorship.

c-thought-wellhausen.text: In 1878 Julius Wellhausen (1844-1918), professor of the Old Testament at Greifswald from 1872, published a synthesis that established the Documentary Hypothesis as the consensus explanation of the first books of the Bible: a developmental sequence of sources, J, E, D and P, with P dated to the postexilic period. On this view the books were not written by Moses, their laws and rituals were the latest elements, and Israel's religion developed 'from a nomadic religion through the prophets to the law'.
c-thought-wellhausen.label: debated
c-thought-wellhausen.note: A scholarly reconstruction, revised since the 1970s (see below) and rejected by those who hold to Mosaic authorship.

c-thought-dh-later.text: Since the 1970s the existence of E has been questioned and J has been dated to the postexilic period; around 2000 European scholars dismissed J as a source in favour of 'numerous written sources and cycles of tradition', while 'many North American scholars steadfastly defend the Documentary Hypothesis'. P is still generally recognized as a principal source.
c-thought-dh-later.label: debated
c-thought-dh-later.note: Broadly, European scholars favour models of many sources and traditions; many North American scholars keep a revised Documentary Hypothesis.

c-thought-levenson.text: Alan Levenson writes that Wellhausen's analysis was 'perfused with the anti-Jewish sentiment prevalent in Bismarck's Second German Reich', which adversely affected the use of the Documentary Hypothesis among Jewish scholars until Yehezkel Kaufmann introduced a Jewish variation on the theory; Solomon Schechter rejected its 'anti-Judaic embellishments' but not the hypothesis altogether.
c-thought-levenson.label: debated
c-thought-levenson.note: Levenson's assessment of Wellhausen's outlook; after Kaufmann, Jewish scholars too adopted versions of the source analysis.

c-thought-reform.text: Reform rabbis from around the United States, called together by Kaufmann Kohler and presided over by Isaac Mayer Wise, met on 16-19 November 1885 in a meeting they declared a continuation of the Philadelphia Conference of 1869 and the German Conference of 1841-46. Their Pittsburgh Platform said of the Mosaic legislation that 'today we accept as binding only its moral laws, and maintain only such ceremonies as elevate and sanctify our lives', and declared: 'We consider ourselves no longer a nation, but a religious community, and therefore expect neither a return to Palestine, nor a sacrificial worship under the sons of Aaron'.
c-thought-reform.label: consensus

c-thought-hirsch.text: Samson Raphael Hirsch (1808-88), a rabbi in Frankfurt am Main and founder of Separatist Orthodoxy, or Neo-Orthodoxy, required 'strict training in the Torah' together with a modern secular education, so that Orthodoxy could withstand the challenge of Reform Judaism; he rejected applying historical methods to the study of the Bible.
c-thought-hirsch.label: consensus

c-thought-frankel.text: Zechariah Frankel called for 'positive-historical Judaism', and in 1854 his 'conservative yet flexible' approach took shape in the Jewish Theological Seminary of Breslau, which he headed. In New York a Jewish Theological Seminary Association opened by January 1887 and was reorganised in 1902; in 1913 Solomon Schechter created the United Synagogue of America. These are the roots of Conservative Judaism.
c-thought-frankel.label: consensus

c-thought-vatican.text: On 18 July 1870 the First Vatican Council, in Pastor aeternus, defined 'as a divinely revealed dogma' that 'when the Roman pontiff speaks EX CATHEDRA', that is, when 'he defines a doctrine concerning faith or morals to be held by the whole church', he possesses the infallibility that Christ willed his church to enjoy. The Franco-Prussian War interrupted the council, which was never resumed nor officially closed.
c-thought-vatican.label: consensus

c-thought-afghani.text: Jamal al-Din al-Afghani (1838-97), born at Asadabad in Persia, was 'a fighter against European domination'; 'some scholars believe that he was not an Afghan but a Persian Shiʿi'. He spent time in Cairo (from 1871), Paris, Iran and Istanbul, where he died; with Muhammad ʿAbduh he published an anti-British newspaper, al-ʿUrwa al-wuthqa.
c-thought-afghani.label: debated
c-thought-afghani.note: His origin is disputed: his name means 'the Afghan', but Britannica gives his birthplace as Asadabad in Persia, and some scholars believe he was a Persian Shiʿi.

c-thought-abduh.text: Muhammad ʿAbduh (1849-1905), who came under al-Afghani's influence in 1872, was exiled after the British occupation of Egypt for his part in the 'Urabi revolt; in Paris in 1884 he helped al-Afghani publish al-ʿUrwa al-wuthqa ('The Firmest Bond'). In theology he 'sought to establish the harmony of reason and revelation'; 'in 1899, with British help, he became muftī of Egypt', and he worked to reform al-Azhar and Egypt's law and education.
c-thought-abduh.label: consensus

c-thought-berger.text: In 1968 the sociologist Peter Berger predicted in the New York Times: 'By the twenty-first century, religious believers are likely to be found only in small sects.' In 1999 he wrote: 'The assumption that we live in a secularised world is false.'
c-thought-berger.label: debated
c-thought-berger.note: As reported by Alan Brine (RE Online). Berger's earlier and later statements stand for the two sides of the secularization debate.

pages.title: Revolutions
pages.lede: Between 1776 and 1804 revolutions in North America, France and Haiti declared equal rights or independence. By the Maddison Project's estimates the world economy began to accelerate only after 1820, and GDP per person in Britain and the United States pulled away from those in China and India. This chapter follows both revolutions, and the evidence historians use to measure them.
body: In 1776 the American Declaration of Independence held 'that all men are created equal' (14.2). [[c-amrev-declaration-1776]] In 1789 the French Assembly abolished 'the feudal system' and declared that men are 'born and remain free and equal in rights' (14.3). [[c-frrev-feudal-abolition-1789]] [[c-frrev-rights-of-man-1789]] In Saint-Domingue the enslaved rose in 1791, and in 1804 their leaders declared the independence of Haiti (14.4). [[c-haiti-uprising-1791-toussaint]] [[c-haiti-leclerc-independence-1804]]

The other revolution was economic (14.6). The 2023 update of the Maddison Project finds 'pockets of economic growth' before 1820, but a world economy that 'only started to accelerate after that year'. [[c-mpd-1820-acceleration]] On its figures, GDP per person in the United Kingdom rose from 3,306 international dollars in 1820 to 8,212 in 1913, and in the United States from 2,674 to 10,108, while China's went from 882 to 985 and India's from 937 to 1,073. In 1800 the Netherlands, at 4,184, stood above the United Kingdom, at 3,343. [[c-mpd-gdppc-1750-1913]]

How do we know? Partly from censuses. The United States held its first census in 1790, a simple headcount used to share out seats in the House of Representatives. [[c-census-us-1790]] Britain's first census, in 1801, found 8.9 million people in England and Wales, leaving out those at sea, in the military and in prison. [[c-census-gb-1801]]

Output is harder to count. For most of this period no official statistics fully cover GDP, so economic historians reconstruct it, often indirectly from real wages and urbanization. [[c-mpd-indirect-method]] The Maddison Project now covers 169 countries, [[c-mpd-2023-coverage]] but its comparisons depend on the benchmark year used to compare prices, which Bolt and van Zanden defend keeping at 1990, with adjustments, [[c-mpd-benchmark-2025]] and Rafael Guthmann argues that its methods differ between countries and periods. [[c-mpd-guthmann-2025]]

pages.title: The Enlightenment
pages.lede: In 1784 Kant defined enlightenment as humanity's emergence from a 'self-imposed nonage'. Writers from Montesquieu and Rousseau to Adam Smith and Moses Mendelssohn argued about government, trade and freedom of conscience. Historians still dispute how radical the Enlightenment was, and how it regarded race and empire.
body: Kant, writing in 1784, called enlightenment 'man's emergence from his self-imposed nonage' and gave it a motto: Sapere aude, dare to know. [[c-kant-enlightenment-1784]] Its political thought built on Locke, whose Second Treatise is the classical source of modern liberal theory. [[c-locke-liberal-source]] Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748) argued, in Britannica's summary, that the three powers 'must be confided to different individuals or bodies, acting independently', a scheme that shaped James Madison. [[c-montesquieu-spirit-1748]] In William Bristow's summary, Rousseau held that only direct democracy could realize human freedom. [[c-rousseau-direct-democracy]]

Scotland produced its own Enlightenment, with Hutcheson, Adam Smith, Hume and Reid. [[c-scottish-enlightenment]] Smith's The Wealth of Nations (1776) opens with a pin factory in which ten workers, each specializing in a task, turn out 48,000 pins a day, and it attacks the restrictions of what Smith called the 'mercantile system'. [[c-smith-wealth-1776]]

Moses Mendelssohn (1729-1786) translated the Pentateuch and the Psalms into German. In Jerusalem (1783), as Daniel Dahlstrom puts it, he argued that 'neither the state nor religion can legitimately coerce human conscience', and in 1784 he wrote his own essay on what it means to enlighten. [[c-mendelssohn-jerusalem-1783]]

Historians argue over what the Enlightenment was. Jonathan Israel divides it into a 'radical' camp, following Spinoza, and a 'moderate' one; Anthony La Vopa calls this an 'oversimplified classification' and Israel's method 'fundamentally unhistorical'. [[c-israel-radical-moderate]] Its record on race and empire is also disputed. William Bristow writes that its writings are 'rife with rank ethno- and Eurocentrism, often explicit', [[c-enlightenment-eurocentrism]] yet Sankar Muthu argues that Diderot, Kant and Herder defended the freedom of non-European peoples to order their own societies, [[c-muthu-against-empire]] and Pauline Kleingeld argues that Kant himself 'radically changed his mind' about race in the 1790s. [[c-kleingeld-kant-race]]
