pages.title: The American Revolution
pages.lede: After 1763 colonial dissent grew, and in 1776 the Declaration of Independence held that 'all men are created equal'. The Constitution of 1787 counted enslaved people as 'three fifths of all other Persons' and barred a ban on the slave trade before 1808; the Bill of Rights followed in 1791. Historians still dispute what the Revolution was about.
body: The Proclamation of 7 October 1763 stopped grants of land west of the Appalachians; Max Edelson sees it as the beginning of 'escalating colonial dissent'. [[c-amrev-proclamation-1763]] The Declaration of Independence, dated 4 July 1776, held 'that all men are created equal', and accused the King of inciting 'the merciless Indian Savages'. [[c-amrev-declaration-1776]]

The Constitution, signed on 17 September 1787, counted 'three fifths of all other Persons', that is, enslaved people, in apportioning representatives and direct taxes, and left out 'Indians not taxed'. It barred Congress from banning the slave trade before 1808 and required escaped people 'held to Service or Labour' to be returned. [[c-amrev-constitution-slavery-1787]] Sean Wilentz argues that the framers chose to abide slavery without legitimizing it; David Waldstreicher, that slavery mattered as much to the Constitution as the Constitution did to slavery's survival. [[c-amrev-constitution-slavery-debate]]

The Bill of Rights was ratified on 15 December 1791; its First Amendment forbids Congress to make any law 'respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the free exercise thereof'. [[c-amrev-bill-of-rights-1791]] Not everyone stayed for the new republic: by Maya Jasanoff's estimate some 60,000 loyalists fled, taking 15,000 slaves with them. [[c-amrev-loyalist-exodus]]

Interpretations differ. Bernard Bailyn (1967) argued that the Revolutionary leaders' fears of 'slavery' and conspiracy were sincere, drawn from British opposition thought. [[c-amrev-bailyn-1967]] In its publisher's words, Gordon Wood's The Radicalism of the American Revolution argues that the Revolution 'transformed an almost feudal society into a democratic one'. [[c-amrev-wood-radicalism]] R. R. Palmer placed it in a wider Western age of democratic revolution (14.3). [[c-amrev-palmer-atlantic]] The 1619 Project's lead essay, as the Times later summarised it, gave protecting slavery as 'one primary reason' the colonists fought the Revolution. Five historians, including Wilentz and Wood, read this as a claim that independence was declared to ensure slavery would continue and called it 'not true'; the New York Times narrowed the wording to 'a primary motivation for some of the colonists'. [[c-amrev-1619-dispute]]

pages.title: The French Revolution
pages.lede: In August 1789 the Assembly abolished the feudal system and declared that men are 'born and remain free and equal in rights', and in 1791 it removed the last exceptions to the rights of Jews. In 1793-94 the Terror officially executed about 17,000 people. Historians still argue over the death toll in the Vendée and over what kind of revolution this was.
body: After the night of 4 August 1789, the Assembly's decree of 11 August declared that it 'completely abolishes the feudal system'. [[c-frrev-feudal-abolition-1789]] The first article of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (26 August) declared that 'Men are born and remain free and equal in rights', and its tenth article protected religious opinions. [[c-frrev-rights-of-man-1789]]

Did those rights include Jews? On 23 December 1789 Clermont-Tonnerre answered: 'We must refuse everything to the Jews as a nation and accord everything to Jews as individuals.' [[c-frrev-clermont-tonnerre-1789]] On 27 September 1791 the Assembly revoked every remaining exception relating to Jews who swore the civic oath. [[c-frrev-jewish-emancipation-1791]] In 1794 the Convention also abolished slavery in the colonies (14.4). [[c-haiti-french-abolition-1794]]

Under the Terror, from September 1793 to July 1794, about 17,000 people were officially executed, perhaps 10,000 more died in prison or without trial, and at least 300,000 were arrested; it ended with Robespierre's fall on 9 Thermidor. [[c-frrev-terror-toll]] In the Vendée, estimates vary widely: Jean-Clément Martin's runs to up to 250,000 insurgents and 200,000 republicans, while Peter McPhee rejects Pierre Chaunu's 500,000 rebel deaths and calls Reynald Secher's own estimate 'far lower, if still massive'. Secher calls the repression genocide; McPhee replies that huge numbers were killed, but that 'It was not a genocide'. [[c-frrev-vendee-toll]]

What kind of revolution was it? Georges Lefebvre (1939) divided 1789 into four revolutions, aristocratic, bourgeois, popular and peasant, and, as his publisher puts it, wrote history 'from below'. [[c-frrev-lefebvre-social]] Alfred Cobban (1964) challenged such social explanations, and François Furet (English edition, 1981) distinguished between commemorative and conceptual history. [[c-frrev-revisionists]]

pages.title: Haiti, abolition and the Atlantic
pages.lede: In 1791 the enslaved of Saint-Domingue rose, and in 1804 their leaders declared the independence of Haiti. In 1825 Haiti was charged an indemnity of 150 million francs, whose cost is still disputed. Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807 and slavery from 1834, and historians argue over the part economics played.
body: In 1789 Saint-Domingue held roughly 465,000 to 500,000 enslaved people, about 30,000 whites and a similar number of free people of colour. [[c-haiti-saint-domingue-1789]] In August 1791 thousands of the enslaved rose in rebellion. [[c-haiti-uprising-1791-toussaint]] On 4 February 1794 the National Convention abolished slavery in all the French colonies. [[c-haiti-french-abolition-1794]]

Toussaint Louverture made himself governor-general for life in 1801; seized by the French, he died in April 1803. [[c-haiti-uprising-1791-toussaint]] Leclerc's expedition of about 40,000 men was ruined by fighting and yellow fever, Dessalines won at Vertières, and on 1 January 1804 he declared Haiti independent; the French failure contributed to the Louisiana Purchase. [[c-haiti-leclerc-independence-1804]] Philippe Girard writes that the victors then 'eradicated Haiti's white population', calls this genocide, and asks that it be read in its Haitian context. [[c-haiti-1804-killings]]

In 1825 Haiti was charged an indemnity of 150 million francs, later cut to 90 million; combined with loans, it became a double debt. [[c-haiti-indemnity-1825]] Haiti made its last payment on the indemnity in 1878, partly with a loan raised in France in 1875, and the loans of the double debt were paid off in 1888; Britannica gives 1887 as the year the payments were scheduled to end. [[c-haiti-indemnity-payoff]] The New York Times (2022) estimated that the payments cost Haiti between $21 billion and $115 billion in lost growth; [[c-haiti-ransom-nyt-2022]] two economists and two legal scholars, who put the initial debt at nearly 280% of GDP, estimate its cost at between $3 billion and $50 billion; their scenarios run from about $1.6 billion to $1.1 trillion, and they give reasons why their figures may overstate the cost and others why they may understate it. [[c-haiti-debt-cepr-2021]] Some critics said the story was already known. [[c-haiti-ransom-critique]] In 2025 President Macron said that the decision of 1825 placed a price on freedom and set up a joint commission of historians, without offering reparations. [[c-haiti-macron-2025]]

Britain abolished its slave trade in 1807 and slavery itself from 1 August 1834, with apprenticeship until 1838 and £20 million paid to slave-owners. [[c-british-abolition-1807-1833]] Why? Eric Williams argued that slavery's profits fed British industry and that abolition followed its decline. [[c-williams-thesis-1944]] Seymour Drescher replied that abolition came while slavery was still valuable and harmed Britain's economic interests. [[c-drescher-econocide-1977]] Heblich, Redding and Voth (2022) find that slave wealth raised British income by about a decade's growth, reviving the first half of Williams's thesis. [[c-hrv-slavery-wealth-2022]]

pages.title: Napoleon and Latin American independence
pages.lede: In 1808 Napoleon forced Spain's kings to abdicate and chose his brother Joseph to rule Spain. Between 1808 and 1826 all of Latin America except Cuba and Puerto Rico broke away from Spain and Portugal, and Brazil crowned an emperor of its own. Economists still disagree about whether the decades that followed were 'lost'.
body: Napoleon's Civil Code of 1804 swept away hereditary nobility and the privileges of class, but it subordinated women to their fathers and husbands. [[c-latam-code]] In the 19th century a number of European and Latin American countries adopted it of their own accord. [[c-latam-code-adopt]] (For the Revolution that came before Napoleon, see 14.3.)

In 1808 Napoleon turned on Spain. The people of Madrid rose against the French on 2 May; three days later, at Bayonne, Napoleon forced Ferdinand VII and his father Charles IV to give up the crown, and chose his brother Joseph to rule. [[c-latam-bayonne]] Spaniards free of French rule adopted a liberal constitution at Cádiz in 1812, which declared Spain's American possessions full members of the kingdom, not mere colonies. Yet Creoles in the Cortes were denied equal representation, [[c-latam-cadiz]] and on his return in 1814 Ferdinand abolished the Cortes and all its works. [[c-latam-1814]]

In New Spain, Miguel Hidalgo called for revolt at Dolores on 16 September 1810 and raised a large popular army; he was executed the next July. [[c-latam-hidalgo]] In November 1813 José María Morelos's Congress of Chilpancingo declared Mexico independent, but Morelos too was captured and shot. [[c-latam-morelos]] In the south, San Martín crossed the Andes and won at Chacabuco in 1817, [[c-latam-chacabuco]] Bolívar freed New Granada at Boyacá in 1819, [[c-latam-boyaca]] and Sucre's victory at Ayacucho in 1824 secured the independence of the South American republics. [[c-latam-ayacucho]] By 1826 Spain kept only Cuba and Puerto Rico in the Americas. [[c-latam-loss]] Brazil followed a different path. The Portuguese court had moved to Rio in 1808, and in 1822 Pedro proclaimed independence and was crowned emperor. [[c-latam-brazil]]

What did independence do to the economy? Bates, Coatsworth and Williamson argue that in Latin America, as later in Africa, it brought about half a century of instability, violent conflict and stagnation. [[c-latam-lost]] Prados de la Escosura replies that per capita income grew, and that the region fell behind the US and Western Europe but not the rest of the world. In his view, 'lost decades' is an unwarranted description of 1820-1870. [[c-latam-prados]] (For Latin America's later export economies, see 14.13.)

pages.title: The Industrial Revolution in Britain
pages.lede: The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the 18th century. Economists have revised its growth rates downward, and they still argue about why it happened there first, whether it raised workers' living standards, and when Europe pulled ahead of China.
body: Arnold Toynbee used the term 'Industrial Revolution' for Britain's economic development between 1760 and 1840. [[c-ir-start]] In 1769 the Scottish engineer James Watt patented his separate condenser, which vastly improved the efficiency of the steam engine. [[c-ir-watt]]

How fast did the economy grow? Antràs and Voth's table of estimates shows Feinstein (1981) putting output growth in England at 1.1% a year in 1760-1800 and 2.7% in 1801-31. Crafts and Harley (1992) put it at about 1% and 1.9%. [[c-ir-growth]] Their revision made the revolution look more gradual, but they still call it an important discontinuity. [[c-ir-gradual]]

Why Britain? Robert Allen argues that high wages and cheap capital and energy made labour-saving machines uniquely profitable to invent and use there. [[c-ir-allen]] Jane Humphries and Benjamin Schneider find no high-wage economy in spinning, a leading sector, [[c-ir-humphries]] and Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda find that industry grew where wages were low but mechanical skills were high. [[c-ir-kmo]] Allen, answering an earlier critique by Humphries, has presented new evidence that women and children took part in the high-wage economy. [[c-ir-allen-2015]] Emma Griffin, reviewing his book, finds that he has 'convincingly argued' that high wages and cheap fuel deserve 'a central place', though she doubts that any single explanation will do. [[c-ir-griffin]]

Did workers gain? Charles Feinstein found that the average working-class family's standard of living rose by less than 15% between the 1780s and 1850s. [[c-ir-feinstein]] Kelly, Mokyr and Ó Gráda find that real wages rose sharply in the industrial north but fell in the south. [[c-ir-regional]] Kenneth Pomeranz argues that coal and American imports let Britain escape the limits of its land, and he now concedes that his claim of rough parity with the Yangzi delta is stronger for 1750 than for 1800. [[c-ir-pomeranz]] Broadberry, Guan and Li date the divergence between his view and older Eurocentric ones. [[c-ir-bgl]]

pages.title: Industry spreads and the social question
pages.lede: Steam railways opened in England in 1825 and in Belgium by 1835, and Belgium, Germany, the United States and Meiji Japan built industries of their own. Britain extended its limits on child labour and appointed factory inspectors, Marx and Engels published their Manifesto in the year of Europe's revolutions, and Bismarck's Germany created the first old-age social insurance.
body: The Stockton and Darlington, a steam-hauled public railway, opened in 1825, and the Liverpool and Manchester, the world's first inter-city line, followed in 1830. [[c-ind-rail]] Belgium, where machine shops were growing at Liège from about 1807, became the first country in continental Europe to be transformed economically, and in 1835 a train ran from Brussels to Mechelen. [[c-ind-belgium]] In Britannica's account, France industrialised more slowly and Germany expanded after unification (1870-71), though the economic historian John Munro sees 'much more rapid growth and discernible industrialization' from the 1850s; the United States later far outstripped Europe. [[c-ind-germany-us]] In Japan the Meiji government founded the Tomioka silk mill in 1872 with French machinery, and by the beginning of the 20th century Japan was the world's leading exporter of raw silk. [[c-ind-tomioka]] (On Meiji Japan, see 14.10.)

Britain's Factory Act of 1833 barred children under nine from factories, limited the hours of older children, required schooling for those under 13, and created a four-man inspectorate to enforce the rules. [[c-ind-factoryact]] In February 1848 Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published the Manifesto of the Communist Party, which opens: 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.' [[c-ind-manifesto]]

That same year revolution began in Sicily in January, spread across Europe after the revolution of 24 February in France, and, in Britannica's judgement, 'ended in failure and repression', although some reforms lasted, among them the emancipation of the peasants in Austria and the end of absolute monarchy in Denmark. [[c-ind-1848]] In the 1880s Bismarck's Germany introduced sickness insurance, workers' compensation and, in 1889, the world's first old-age insurance, with a pension age of 70. [[c-ind-bismarck]] The Social Security Administration's history says Bismarck wanted both to promote workers' well-being and to head off more radical socialist demands. [[c-ind-motives]]

pages.title: Nations and nationalism
pages.lede: Italy became a kingdom in 1861, and the German Empire was proclaimed in 1871. In the same decades racial antisemitism took shape, pogroms struck the Jews of the Russian empire, the Jewish officer Alfred Dreyfus was convicted of treason in France, and in 1897 the First Zionist Congress met at Basel. Scholars still debate whether nations are modern creations or have older roots.
body: The Kingdom of Italy was established in 1861, and it annexed Venetia in 1866 and papal Rome in 1870. [[c-nat-italy]] On 18 January 1871 the German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles. [[c-nat-germany]]

Where do nations come from? For the modernist Ernest Gellner, 'the world was created round about the end of the eighteenth century'. Anthony Smith stressed ethnic roots, and when the two debated at Warwick in 1995 Gellner called such continuity 'inessential'. [[c-nat-gellner]] Benedict Anderson called the nation 'imagined', because its members never meet most of their fellow-members, [[c-nat-anderson]] and Eric Hobsbawm and Terence Ranger argued that many supposedly ancient traditions had been invented recently. [[c-nat-hobsbawm]]

In the 1870s Wilhelm Marr is credited with coining the word 'antisemitism', and racial antisemitism took shape in the late 19th century. [[c-nat-marr]] In the Russian empire pogroms began at Yelizavetgrad in 1881, and the restrictive May Laws followed in 1882. [[c-nat-pogroms]] At Kishinev in 1903 a pogrom left about 45 to 49 Jews dead (45 by the Encyclopaedia Judaica's count, 49 in the description of Steven Zipperstein's study) and hundreds wounded. [[c-nat-kishinev]] In France the army captain Alfred Dreyfus, who was Jewish, was convicted of treason in 1894. Émile Zola took up his case, but the army did not publicly declare him innocent until 1995. [[c-nat-dreyfus]]

In 1896 Theodor Herzl called for 'the restoration of the Jewish State'. [[c-nat-herzl]] Herzl later said the Dreyfus affair had made him a Zionist; Shlomo Avineri points instead to his long analysis of the failure of emancipation. [[c-nat-herzl-dreyfus]] The First Zionist Congress met at Basel in 1897 and sought a home for the Jewish people secured by public law. [[c-nat-basel]] For those who identify as Zionists, as the description of Derek Penslar's study puts it, the word connotes liberation; for others it is a source of distaste. Britannica notes that under the British Mandate, in the 1920s and 1930s, Palestine's Arab population feared that the land would eventually become a Jewish state, and Penslar's study of 2023 offers a new take on the movement's relationship to colonialism. [[c-nat-zionism-meaning]] (See 14.12.)

pages.title: Emancipations
pages.lede: Between 1861 and 1888 Russia freed its serfs, and the United States, Cuba and Brazil abolished slavery. Freedom often came with conditions, and in 1877 federal troops left three Southern states, ending Reconstruction there. Economists and historians still argue about what slavery meant for economic growth.
body: By Alexander II's Emancipation Manifesto of 3 March 1861, Russia's serfs were freed. They were organised in village communities and were to repay the state over 49 years for the land they received. [[c-eman-russia]] Emancipation freed roughly 40 percent of the population from bondage, but the reforms left the empire's political structure unchanged. [[c-eman-share]]

In the United States, Lincoln's Emancipation Proclamation of 1863 did not end slavery in the nation. The Thirteenth Amendment, passed at the end of the Civil War and ratified in December 1865, did. [[c-eman-13th]] After the disputed election of 1876, what 64 Parishes calls an unwritten deal, the Compromise of 1877, though some historians doubt that a bargain was struck, secured the presidency for Rutherford B. Hayes, and federal troops were removed from Florida, Louisiana and South Carolina, effectively ending Reconstruction there. [[c-eman-1877]] Cuba replaced slavery in 1880 with the patronato, a transition meant to last eight years, and ended it early in 1886. [[c-eman-cuba]] Brazil abolished slavery outright in 1888, without compensation to the owners. [[c-eman-brazil]] (On Haiti and British abolition, see 14.4.)

Was slavery economically doomed? Robert Fogel and Stanley Engerman argued in 1974 that slavery, 'in spite of its inhumanity', had been efficient, and that it ended because of political decisions rather than economic weakness. Their book provoked bitter controversy. [[c-eman-fogel]] Herbert Gutman, Paul David and others attacked it from several directions. [[c-eman-critics]] More recently, historians of the 'new history of capitalism' have tied industrial capitalism to slave-grown cotton. Alan Olmstead and Paul Rhode reply that they mishandle the evidence. [[c-eman-nhc]]

pages.title: China and Japan
pages.lede: Britain fought China over the opium trade in 1839-42, and Britain and France fought it again in 1856-60, while the Taiping rebellion cost tens of millions of lives. Japan's new imperial government abolished the feudal domains and brought in conscription, and Japan went on to defeat China in 1894-95 and Russia in 1904-05.
body: Foreign traders, mainly British, had been exporting opium illegally from India to China since the 18th century. When the Chinese government confiscated and destroyed more than 20,000 chests of it at Canton, Britain went to war: the first Opium War lasted from 1839 to 1842, and Britain and France fought a second from 1856 to 1860. [[c-qing-opium-wars]] The Treaty of Nanjing (1842) made China pay Britain a large indemnity, cede Hong Kong Island and open five treaty ports to British trade and residence instead of one. [[c-qing-nanjing]] In 1858 the importation of opium was legalized, and in 1860 British and French troops captured Beijing and plundered and burned the Yuanming Garden, the emperor's summer palace. [[c-qing-1860]] (On the Qing to 1722, see 13.11.)

Meanwhile the Taiping rebellion (1850-64) was led by Hong Xiuquan, a disappointed candidate in the civil-service examinations who believed himself the son of God and the younger brother of Jesus Christ. In 1853 his followers took Nanjing and renamed it Tianjing, 'Heavenly Capital'; it fell in July 1864. [[c-qing-hong]] Forces organised under the Qing official Zeng Guofan fought the Taipings, as did a Western-trained 'Ever-Victorious Army', led first by the American Frederick Townsend Ward and then by the British officer Charles Gordon. [[c-qing-taiping-suppress]] Estimates of the dead vary. Britannica gives an estimated 20 million and a page on Tobie Meyer-Fong's study of the war's aftermath some 30 million; a popular history says conservative estimates start at 20 to 30 million and that much of the mortality came from disease and famine rather than fighting. [[c-qing-taiping-toll]]

From 1861 Zeng Guofan, Li Hongzhang and Zuo Zongtang tried to consolidate Qing power by introducing Western technology. Britannica credits this Self-Strengthening movement with some notable gains but judges its overall success limited. [[c-qing-selfstr]] In Japan, the Meiji Restoration brought down the Tokugawa shogunate and restored direct imperial rule. [[c-qing-meiji]] The new government declared feudalism abolished in 1871, turning nearly 300 fiefs into 72 prefectures and 3 metropolitan districts; it introduced nationwide conscription in 1873 and set the land tax at 3 percent of the land's assessed value. [[c-qing-meiji-reforms]] (On Japan's industrial drive, see 14.7.)

Rivalry over Korea brought war between China and Japan in 1894. At Shimonoseki in 1895 China recognized Korea's independence, ceded Taiwan, the Pescadores and the Liaodong Peninsula, and agreed to pay a large indemnity, but Russia, France and Germany forced Japan to hand Liaodong back. [[c-qing-sinojap]] Three years later Russia pressed China into leasing it Port Arthur, at the peninsula's tip. [[c-qing-portarthur]] In 1900 the Boxers, a secret society encouraged by the empress dowager Cixi, attacked Chinese Christians and Western missionaries and besieged the foreign legations in Beijing until an international force of some 19,000 troops took the city on 14 August. [[c-qing-boxer-rising]] The protocol of 1901 imposed an indemnity of 450 million Haikwan taels at 4 percent interest, to be paid off by the end of 1940. [[c-qing-boxer]] In 1904-05 Japan fought Russia over Korea and Manchuria and became, in Britannica's words, 'the first Asian power in modern times to defeat a European power'. [[c-qing-russojap]]

pages.title: Empire in India and Africa
pages.lede: After the rising of 1857-58 the British Crown took over the East India Company's rule in India, and in 1876-78 famine killed an estimated 5.5 million people in the south, on Mike Davis's figures. In Africa, Leopold II's Congo Free State ran on forced labour, and Germany waged a war on the Herero and Nama that it recognised as genocide in 2021. Scholars still argue over how many died under British rule in India and over who gained from empire.
body: The rising of 1857-58 began among the East India Company's Indian troops, the sepoys, at Meerut, and spread to Delhi, Agra, Kanpur and Lucknow. [[c-raj-1857]] Its name is disputed: Britannica files it under 'Indian Mutiny', but in India it is often called the First War of Independence, and Britannica itself warns that 'To regard the rebellion merely as a sepoy mutiny is to underestimate the root causes leading to it'. [[c-raj-1857-causes]] In August 1858 Parliament transferred British power over India from the Company to the Crown, beginning the Raj, which lasted until 1947; in 1876 Queen Victoria took the title Empress of India. [[c-raj-crown]] In the famine of 1876-78 an estimated 5.5 million people in South and Southwestern India died of starvation; the V&A, following Mike Davis, blames drought but also the colonial government's export of grain. [[c-raj-famine]] As crops failed in 1876, the viceroy, Lord Lytton, was organising the Imperial Assemblage at Delhi, with 'a week-long feast for 68,000 officials, satraps and maharajas'. [[c-raj-lytton]]

How many died under British rule is now argued over. Dylan Sullivan and Jason Hickel (2023) measure deaths against the average death rate of 16th- and 17th-century England and find '165 million excess deaths in India between 1880 and 1920'; against India's own death rate in the 1880s, they find about 50 million for 1891-1920. [[c-raj-sh]] Tirthankar Roy replies that 'The British Raj did not start the famines. Geography did.' Monsoon failure struck the drier Deccan, not the north, and he credits railways, trade and a more capable state with the sharp fall in deaths after 1901. In a scholarly paper of 2016 he argued that a mainly geographical account understates the state's role in famines, and a mainly political one overstates it. [[c-raj-roy]] The two sides also differ over money. Utsa Patnaik, as Hickel reports, puts the 'drain' of wealth from India in 1765-1938, with interest of about 5 percent a year compounded to the present, at $44.6 trillion, a claim Roy calls 'based on dreadfully bad economics and is still untestable'. [[c-raj-drain]] Lance Davis and Robert Huttenback asked whether empire paid Britain. They found empire investment profitable before 1880 but not, afterwards, compared with home and foreign investment; its returns rested on subsidies paid by British taxpayers, and the imperial experience could be viewed 'more as a redistribution of income within the United Kingdom', from the middle class to the elites. [[c-raj-dh]] (On the Great Divergence, see 14.6.)

In Africa, a conference at Berlin (November 1884 to February 1885), proposed by Portugal, dealt with the Congo River basin; its act 'guaranteed freedom for trade and shipping for all states in the basin' and forbade slave trading. [[c-raj-berlin]] The Congo Free State (1885-1908), with its capital at Boma from 1886, [[c-raj-boma]] was a private holding under Leopold II's 'unrestrained personal control'. Forced labour gathered wild rubber, palm oil and ivory, and Force Publique troops cut off the hands of Congolese, including children; after a campaign by the British-founded Congo Reform Association, the state was replaced in 1908 by the Belgian Congo, under the Belgian parliament. [[c-raj-congo]] Its population is said to have fallen from some 20 million to 8 million. [[c-raj-congo-pop]]

In South West Africa, today's Namibia, German forces defeated the Herero at the Waterberg on 11-12 August 1904 and drove the survivors into the waterless Omaheke, where thousands died of thirst; General Lothar von Trotha called for the extermination of the population. [[c-raj-herero]] Historians cited by the Associated Press estimate that about 65,000 Herero and at least 10,000 Nama were killed; the German Historical Museum gives 35 to 80 percent of some 40,000 to 100,000 Herero and up to half of about 22,000 Nama. About 1,750 Germans died. [[c-raj-herero-toll]] In 2021 Germany's foreign minister, Heiko Maas, said Germany would 'now officially call these events what they were from today's perspective: a genocide', and offered 1.1 billion euros over 30 years, largely for development, while insisting that 'legal claims to compensation cannot be derived from this'. [[c-raj-2021]] Laidlaw Peringanda of the Namibian Genocide Association rejected the offer, and on Namibia's first genocide remembrance day, 28 May 2025, its president said the government would continue to push for reparations. [[c-raj-2025]]

pages.title: The Ottoman empire and the Middle East
pages.lede: Ottoman sultans proclaimed reforms and a constitution, and Muhammad Ali reorganised Egypt's land and army, but Egypt's debts brought European control of its finances and, in 1882, British occupation. Constitutions came to Istanbul in 1876 and again in 1908 and to Iran in 1906, while Jewish immigrants arrived in Ottoman Palestine, where Jews remained a small minority.
body: Muhammad Ali, named the Ottoman sultan's viceroy in Egypt in 1805, turned most of Egypt's farmland into state land by 1815, introduced cash crops such as cotton, and built a fleet and an army of conscripted peasants; but his industrial experiments failed, largely because Egypt lacked sources of power. [[c-ott-muhammadali]] In the Ottoman empire the Tanzimat reforms (1839-76) began with the Gülhane edict of 1839, which promised 'security of life, property, and honour to all subjects of the empire', a standard system of taxation and fairer conscription; yet the promises of equality for non-Muslims, mainly Christians and Jews, 'were not always carried out'. [[c-ott-tanzimat]] (On the Ottomans to 1722, see 13.10.)

Abdülhamid II promulgated the first Ottoman constitution on 23 December 1876, but in February 1878 he suspended it and dismissed the parliament. [[c-ott-1876]] In July 1908 officers of the III Army Corps in Macedonia demanded 'the immediate restoration of the 1876 constitution' and got it; after a short-lived reactionary uprising in April 1909 Abdülhamid was deposed, and in 1913 the Committee of Union and Progress took over the government. [[c-ott-youngturk]] Iran had its own Constitutional Revolution. Protests began in December 1905; after a sanctuary at the British legation in July 1906 the shah granted a decree in August, and a constitution was adopted that December. Mohammad-ʿAli Shah's coup of June 1908 began a 'lesser tyranny' until the constitution was restored in July 1909, and in December 1911, after a joint ultimatum and the expulsion of the American financial adviser Morgan Shuster, the Second Majles was dissolved. [[c-ott-iran]]

The Suez Canal opened to shipping on 17 November 1869. Debts forced Isma'il Pasha to put Egypt's shares in the canal company up for sale, and in 1875 Disraeli's government bought them with £4 million advanced by the Rothschilds. [[c-ott-suez]] Expensive projects such as the canal left Egypt bankrupt in 1876; it accepted British and French control of its revenues, which assigned 60 percent of them to paying its creditors. [[c-ott-egyptdebt]] A movement led by 'Urabi then sought to place the khedive, Tawfiq, under constitutional rule. After riots in Alexandria in June 1882 Britain invaded to restore Tawfiq's power, won a battle at Tel al-Kabir that was disastrous for the Egyptians, and occupied the country. [[c-ott-urabi]]

In Ottoman Palestine, the First Aliyah (usually dated 1882-1904) brought about 30,000 young Jews from Europe and Yemen, amid the upheaval that followed the Russian pogroms of 1881-82 (14.8). The first colonies of the period included Rishon Lezion, Zichron Yaacov, Rosh Pina and Petah Tikva, though Petah Tikva had been founded earlier, in 1878; their most prominent benefactor was Baron Edmond de Rothschild. [[c-ott-aliyah1]] The Second Aliyah (1904-14) brought about 35,000 more, mostly from Eastern Europe. They prized 'Hebrew labor', though many farmers kept hiring Arab workers, and in 1909 a lottery assigned the plots of what became Tel Aviv; at least half of these immigrants left within a few years. [[c-ott-aliyah2]] Estimates of the Jewish population in 1914 run from 38,754 Jewish Ottoman subjects through Justin McCarthy's 60,000 to 85,000 or more, in a total population that McCarthy puts at 722,143; [[c-ott-pop]] another table gives about 525,000 Muslims, 94,000 Jews and 70,000 Christians and others. [[c-ott-pop-jvl]] On every estimate of the Jewish population, Jews were a small minority, between about 8 and 14 percent; Jewish Ottoman subjects alone were about 5 percent. [[c-ott-minority]]

pages.title: The first globalization
pages.lede: From the 1860s steamships, railways, the Suez Canal and the telegraph cut the cost and time of moving goods and news, and country after country tied its money to gold. Tens of millions migrated, from Europe to the Americas and from India and southern China across Asia, while Argentina drew millions of immigrants and Porfirian Mexico drew foreign capital.
body: Kevin O'Rourke and Jeffrey Williamson find 'a very big globalization bang' in the 19th century (13.6). [[c-glob-bang]] Steamships and the Suez Canal linked continents and railways reached into their interiors (14.7, 14.12), and the North freight-rate index fell by 'more than 41 percent, in real terms' between 1870 and 1910. [[c-glob-freight]] Prices converged: wheat in Liverpool, which cost 57.6 percent more than in Chicago in 1870, cost only 17.8 percent more in 1895 and 15.6 percent more in 1912. [[c-glob-wheat]]

News moved faster still. In July 1866 a cable joined Ireland and Newfoundland, and messages that had taken 10 days by ship now crossed 'in a matter of minutes'. [[c-glob-cable]] Money was linked too. Britain had formally adopted the gold standard in 1816; 'the rush to the gold standard occurred in the 1870s', as Germany, the Scandinavian countries, France and others joined, and the United States had a legal as well as an effective gold standard from 1879. The system broke down when war came in August 1914. [[c-glob-gold]]

People moved on a vast scale. One textbook table puts long-distance migration in 1846-1940 at 55-58 million from Europe to the Americas, 48-52 million from India and southern China to Southeast Asia, the Indian Ocean rim and the South Pacific, and 46-51 million from Northeast Asia and Russia into Manchuria, Siberia, Central Asia and Japan. [[c-glob-ranges]] The historian Adam McKeown notes that the United States and Southeast Asia received 39 and 35 million migrant arrivals in 1870-1930, and he faults the economists Timothy Hatton and Jeffrey Williamson for 'the common error of assuming that indentured migration accounts for the bulk of Asian migrations'. [[c-glob-mckeown]] Many went home again: of 30 million who left India in 1834-1937, no fewer than 24 million returned. [[c-glob-india-return]] Indenture still mattered: almost half a million indentured Indians landed at the Aapravasi Ghat in Mauritius alone between 1834 and 1920, the site of what the British government called 'the great experiment' in using 'free' labour to replace slaves, and the last indentured labourers went to the West Indies in 1916. [[c-glob-indenture]]

Argentina received 5.9 million immigrants between 1870 and 1914, more than half of whom stayed; most came from Italy and Spain, and by 1914 the foreign-born were 30 percent of the population and 50 percent in Buenos Aires. [[c-glob-argentina]] That share was higher than Canada's, Australia's or the United States'. Around 1895 Italians were 51 percent and Spaniards 23 percent of immigrants to Buenos Aires, and Spaniards earned seven to ten percent less; Leticia Arroyo Abad, Noel Maurer and Blanca Sánchez-Alonso suggest that 'individualistic Spanish immigrants viewed each other as competitors for the same jobs, not compatriots to be helped'. [[c-glob-ba]] In Mexico, Porfirio Díaz, president from 1877 and again from 1884, encouraged foreigners to build railroads, dig mines and irrigate fields, but 'most of the profits went abroad or stayed in the hands of a very few wealthy Mexicans'; when revolution came his government collapsed, and he resigned on 25 May 1911. [[c-glob-diaz]]

pages.title: Science, religion and modern thought
pages.lede: Lyell argued that the earth was very ancient and Darwin that humans and animals share a common ancestry, while Wellhausen dated the sources of the Pentateuch and placed its law after the prophets. New Jewish movements took shape, the First Vatican Council defined papal infallibility, and Muslim reformers sought to reconcile reason and revelation.
body: Charles Lyell's Principles of Geology (1830-33) explained the earth's features by ordinary processes working slowly, which meant that the earth must be very ancient; Darwin wrote of 'the wonderful superiority of Lyell's manner of treating geology'. [[c-thought-lyell]] Darwin's On the Origin of Species (1859) 'at first shocked religious Victorian society' by suggesting that animals and humans shared a common ancestry, but his nonreligious biology appealed to the rising class of professional scientists. [[c-thought-darwin]] At the Oxford University Museum on 30 June 1860, Bishop Samuel Wilberforce and the biologist Thomas Huxley clashed before almost 500 people. No one accurately recorded what was said; Huxley is claimed to have retorted, 'I unhesitatingly affirm my preference for the ape.' [[c-thought-oxford]] (On the Scientific Revolution, see 13.12.)

Tradition ascribed the books of the Torah to Moses. [[c-thought-mosaic]] In 1878 Julius Wellhausen, then professor of the Old Testament at Greifswald, published a synthesis that made the Documentary Hypothesis the scholarly consensus: four sources in the order J, E, D and P, with the priestly source P dated after the exile. On this view the books were not written by Moses, their laws and rituals were the latest layer, and Israel's religion developed 'from a nomadic religion through the prophets to the law'. [[c-thought-wellhausen]] Since the 1970s many scholars have questioned whether E existed, and many European scholars have given up J for 'numerous written sources and cycles of tradition', while 'many North American scholars steadfastly defend the Documentary Hypothesis'. [[c-thought-dh-later]] Alan Levenson finds Wellhausen's analysis 'perfused with the anti-Jewish sentiment prevalent in Bismarck's Second German Reich', which held back Jewish scholars' use of the hypothesis until Yehezkel Kaufmann offered a Jewish version of it. [[c-thought-levenson]]

Three Jewish movements took shape (on Moses Mendelssohn, see 14.1). Reform rabbis meeting at Pittsburgh in November 1885, convened by Kaufmann Kohler with Isaac Mayer Wise presiding, traced their gathering back to a German conference of 1841-46. Their platform accepted as binding only the 'moral laws' of the Mosaic legislation and declared, 'We consider ourselves no longer a nation, but a religious community', expecting 'neither a return to Palestine' nor a restored sacrificial worship. [[c-thought-reform]] In Frankfurt am Main, Samson Raphael Hirsch (1808-88), founder of Neo-Orthodoxy, combined 'strict training in the Torah' with modern secular education so that Orthodoxy could withstand Reform. [[c-thought-hirsch]] Zechariah Frankel called for 'positive-historical Judaism' and in 1854 headed a new seminary at Breslau; in New York a Jewish Theological Seminary Association opened in 1887, and in 1913 Solomon Schechter founded the United Synagogue of America, the roots of Conservative Judaism. [[c-thought-frankel]]

On 18 July 1870 the First Vatican Council defined 'as a divinely revealed dogma' that when the pope 'speaks EX CATHEDRA', defining 'a doctrine concerning faith or morals to be held by the whole church', he possesses the infallibility Christ willed his church to have. The Franco-Prussian War interrupted the council, which was never officially closed. [[c-thought-vatican]] Among Muslims, Jamal al-Din al-Afghani (1838-97), whom some scholars believe to have been a Persian Shiʿi rather than an Afghan, fought against European domination [[c-thought-afghani]] and with Muhammad ʿAbduh published an anti-British journal in Paris in 1884. ʿAbduh 'sought to establish the harmony of reason and revelation', and in 1899, with British help, became mufti of Egypt. [[c-thought-abduh]] Sociologists' expectations changed too: in 1968 the sociologist Peter Berger predicted that by the 21st century believers would be found 'only in small sects', but in 1999 he wrote, 'The assumption that we live in a secularised world is false.' [[c-thought-berger]]
